texto: the thing i often find the most frustrating about writing, especially writing fiction with intention of having it published, is the inability to compress the totality of your work and what you're trying to say into something that could hook others in a few minutes as effectively as staring at a canvas or listening to a song. all art forms have a relation to space and time, and how they are engaged with by others in space and time, but differ in the amount of control they have over either or both of those things: a sculpture informs a space, and remains in time, but it can't control if someone walks past it without looking, or the lobby it's located in decides to carve it into pieces and stash it in a warehouse; movies and songs have a completeness of time given that the time it takes you to engage with it is set by the artist, and while movies ideally inform the made-for-purpose space of the theater, and music finds intention of space in both the recording studio and the concert hall, nowadays with device proliferation both lack of control over the space where one watches or listens to it, and often have to share space with the "real" world beyond them; books are finite objects, but have no concrete power to exercise over you when it comes to how long it takes you to read them, where you read them, the quantity of sessions it takes to read them to completion and if you even finish them at all. with some new friends i took a trip to the noguchi museum the other day, which was in the final week of a special exhibition about the works of isamu noguchi specific to new york city, most of which were unrealized, destroyed or altered public works projects. i hadn't found a special exhibition that moving since the gustave caillebotte one at the art institute of chicago , mainly due to how starkly it contrasted with the solemnity and quiet and inscrutability and general rick-owens-runway-backgrounding of the permanent arrangement of the sculptures downstairs: here was a man who committed himself deeply to a city and believed in the transformative potential of labor, only to be rejected in most of his attempts to engender some productive change in his city vis a vis of planned public parks, playgrounds and general art spaces, a lifetime of fighting past this frustration informing the difficulty in "getting" the works downstairs without aide of museum copy, and the intention behind the bespokeness of the museum itself as noguchi's "final gift" to the city. on the train back home one of these new friends (all three of which being musicians, historically the type of artist bonnie is the farthest pole away from in terms of mutual understanding about our art practice and the mechanics behind it) expressed her own frustration at how noguchi's sculpture, and sculpture/museum works of visual art in general, stand so immediately and completely for themselves in a way that music doesn't, to which i laugh and said something to the effect of, "you musicians can achieve something for someone in three minutes what writing would take in three hours!" this was to be the first time i watched a brigher summer day in one continuous sitting (the first time i turned it on too late i got too tired after the first hour, and my first complete viewing was broken up with some pauses here and there), and in a theater, so given the profundity of the day prior at the noguchi, i was expecting to have another totality of artistic experience with a movie already quite dear to me, but four hours came and went and it never fully clicked into place for me, my favorite shots (the lacquered door, honey's entrance, the parallel bike walks between father and son, ming and si'r in the wheat fields, etc) seeming fixed and static. i found myself thinking about nashville , something with a similar quantity of moving parts that fall into place in a final act of public murder, and how the first time i saw nashville in a theater, also a rewatch, my heart could not stop pounding knowing someone was going to die soon and the fact it wouldn't be a surprise this time made it wrench the gut all the more, but a frustration i had with this the first time around that compounded even more here is that the development in si'r's character as acting on a capacity to kill someone is an exponential incongruity compared to the otherwise steady downs and rebounded ups and again downs of the narrative. yang in general is a historical example of mine of a male director with a great sensitivity towards fully realizing female characters, but the women in brighter summer day , despite the gender roles of the point in depicted space and time they occupy, are mostly instrumental and fall in and out of the narrative as needed. granted, this more than any of yang's other films is a Movie About Boys, and certain choices are smart ones, like how ming maintains a strong presence despite a lot of the information presented about her being skewed hearsay from boys and men who are invariably in love with her (beyond the retroactively-revealed-to-be-her flashlighted kiss at the start, we never actually see her *do* any of the fooling around the boys constantly claim of her), but, in the film paced like a three-hour gang epic with an hour rider of bildungsroman family drama at the end, her death, and the perceived necessity of it as a cementing of sir's arc, is perhaps the most senseless in a movie where a handful of teenagers die by the circumstance of samurai sword in near-total darkness. brighter summer day still remains to me one of yang's three works that achieve objective perfection in their filmmaking ( yi yi and a confucian confusion the other two), which i think only makes the flaws to its airtight seals all the more compelling. there has to be a critic out there who's said it better than me but i believe as some sort of universal law that as an artist gets older their work only becomes more and more about their art form of choice itself. consider the next-door movie studio here: it's certainly a space of frustration—the color of the dress is wrong, the actress isn't good enough, ming doesn't find si'r up in the rafters looking back at her—but the scenes here bookend the film in a way, given that si'r's decision to steal the flashlight is what ends up catching sly in the act, which many characters labor to tell si'r as the thing that started the whole mess, and si'r's decision to leave the flashlight back where he found it and replace it in his waistband with the knife the thing that kills ming, kills himself and the narrative in essence: film itself brings this story into existence, and ends it just as suddenly. ( jonathan rosenbaum's piece on yang writes about the flashlight better than i and reading it on the way to the screening really clued me to look out for it in all scenes like a video game key item.) it’s almost like in precisely mapping out every inch of the screen, in taking four years to prepare the filming of such a calibrated machine, yang took it to the limit only to find himself at the fundamental frustration that a limit is something you can never pass beyond; you can only keep making more things and infinitely continue to move forward. brighter summer day 's glass half-emptiness certainly leaves almost no way out for most of its characters—ming and honey are dead, ma loses his best friend, cat's tapes are trashed, si'r is jailed, si'r's father is reduced to a paranoid wifebeater with no promising future employment, si'r's mother is left with an absence she can never fill despite how close she holds it to herself, lao er is without hopes or dreams, even the reverend of the church to which si'r's middle sister devotes herself seems to hold her in some minor disdain—but the one character who seems to have it good in his final scene, uncle fat, is in high spirits because of how si'r saved his life, regardless of si'r's prior expressed want to hurt him. i don't think si'r is particularly a stand-in for yang, as it's based on a real event he had some proximity to in his schoolboy days, but maybe si'r is a version of yang with a similar childhood interest in and proximity to a film, but a version of yang who could not overcome his frustrations, unaware to the fact that regardless of his possible intention to hurt uncle fat that night, something he did saved his life, and uncle fat has a renewed lease on life because of it. so regardless of how frustrating writing is for me, regardless of how frustrating it is to ever make anything, or even do anything, we only do it, we always do it to help someone live just a little longer.

texto: Words cannot fully describe just how disappointed I am that this film did not land for me. For the last sort of three to four years ‘ Aftersun’ has been talked about as one of the most successful directorial debuts ever, and in the same breath one of the most moving films of the decade yet, I’m utterly let down. There were only really a few scenes I was able to honestly resonate with and I don’t believe Charlotte Wells completely unlocks the deeply personal and stagnant emotionality she desires. Fairly dissatisfied with Paul Mescal’s performance in the film too, in fact I feel as though Frankie Corio even outperformed the then 26-year-old which is shocking. It also completely derailed any nuanced meaning for me because the way he acts is a causality and emotional anchor for Corio’s character, so for him to then not prevail in the role was an immediate disaster. I hope that this improves on rewatch, granted I give it a second chance, although I don’t see that being super likely.

texto: why can’t we give ourselves one more chance? this isn’t the actual lyric, but i’ve always misinterpreted it as this and it makes more sense to me. a pretty stunning feature debut from wells, somewhere in between after yang and petite maman. oke moves the camera with all the measured physicality of claire denis and is almost yang-reminiscent in his interest in reflections. i love the confidence on display here and indulgence is great, but i do think that at a certain point, there are negative returns from the overuse of oke’s technique. the way hands and arms and interiors are framed is great at showing sophie’s curiosity at the unfamiliar and her burgeoning adolescence/independence, but i don’t think the composite character study is as successful at picking apart calum through her eyes. his empathy radiates in waves, and the inner turmoil is clear, but it’s missing something. god, the climax though. the kid is great and all hail paul mescal.

texto: Aftersun is one of those films that feels incredibly simple on the surface, yet completely devastating underneath. The performances are so natural that they never feel like acting, they feel like real people, which makes the relationship between Sophie and her dad (Callum) deeply personal and relatable. That ordinary, everyday quality is what makes the film so heartbreaking, because it captures the small moments we often overlook until they become memories. Rather than relying on dramatic events, Aftersun quietly builds an emotional weight that lingers long after it ends, leaving a sense of love, loss and regret that feels painfully human.

texto: Ok, so this took a lot of thinking, but I think I finally made sense of this film. This film made me see that you only know the version of someone that they show to you. The memories you have with or of someone are probably not actually what happened or who they truly are and felt in those moments. Our memories, especially from childhood can often have a rose coloured lense over them because at that time, you weren't aware of things in the grand scheme. You had an innocent mind because you were a kid. Most of my personal childhood memories have gaps. These gaps could have been good events or not so good events, and I'll never know because there was no camera. My siblings probably share the same memories as me, but with less or more gaps, with different details and specifics. My parents probably remember every specific and have no gaps in the memories I have from being a kid. Its like we were all there, at the same event, where we experienced the same thing, but we all probably remember it a little bit different. I probably won't remember writing this review, the same way I don't remember writing most of my reviews after a few weeks. Memory is a weird thing when you think about it. And this movie really made me think about it.

texto: This was a movie which i didnt understand and definitely need to rewatch. Incredible acting from Mescal and Corio. Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

texto: Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

texto: I sat down and watched this twice consecutively tonight. I think part of the beauty of this film is that it takes a minute to get. it’s very beautiful and visually impressive, but the deeper meaning is definitely supposed to be lost to you on your first viewing, seeing as the whole thing happens in Sophie’s imagination. you are living it through her as she tries to piece together her memories of the trip and who her father really was. the symbolism here is insane. there’s definitely more to unpack, but the two that stood out to me were the “rave” scenes being a metaphor for Sophie’s incomplete memories of Calum, and the polaroid photograph that sort of made the movie’s meaning click for me: that the physical media is really all Soph can see when she delves back into her old memories. on my first viewing I didn’t really get it until that moment - I just thought it was very pretty and was unsettled by how clearly disturbed Calum was on his own. but the second time around I cried. this is perfect and takes levels of understanding, which is exactly what I look for in a movie.

texto: Ok, so this took a lot of thinking, but I think I finally made sense of this film. This film made me see that you only know the version of someone that they show to you. The memories you have with or of someone are probably not actually what happened or who they truly are and felt in those moments. Our memories, especially from childhood can often have a rose coloured lense over them because at that time, you weren't aware of things in the grand scheme. You had an innocent mind because you were a kid. Most of my personal childhood memories have gaps. These gaps could have been good events or not so good events, and I'll never know because there was no camera. My siblings probably share the same memories as me, but with less or more gaps, with different details and specifics. My parents probably remember every specific and have no gaps in the memories I have from being a kid. Its like we were all there, at the same event, where we experienced the same thing, but we all probably remember it a little bit different. I probably won't remember writing this review, the same way I don't remember writing most of my reviews after a few weeks. Memory is a weird thing when you think about it. And this movie really made me think about it.

exemplo: As críticas destacam que o filme é extremamente lento, com diálogos que se arrastam e momentos que parecem ser repetidos demais, causando frustração e tédio ao espectador.
texto: c’est un film très lent, avec une atmosphère étrange et de très très très très longs dialogues. c’est un infini procès, avec une embrouille interminable, qui révèle une ambiance très sombre et des personnages tous plus bizarres les uns que les autres. on comprend pas tout et c’est très compliqué d’accrocher. certains plans sont filmées de façon original, et les scènes sont vraiment longues. c’est un film chargé en émotion, avec beaucoup de secrets enfouies. au bout d’un moment ça devient vraiment interminable, des faits surgissent, des hypothèses sont conjecturées, mais c’est jamais explicitement concret. bon ok la façon dont c’est réalisé est très intéressante. par contre, j’ai carrément détesté la fin, pcq tout le long on s’attend à une réponse concrète mais le but du film c’est justement de ne donner aucune réponse, du coup c’est super frustrant. toute l’histoire on peut l’interpréter seulement par des « peut être » et jamais par de véritables faits. chacun des personnages sont intéressants, avec des points de vus différents et des façons de subir la situation différentes, mais le spectateur est à la place des jurés, donc c’est très compliqué de savoir démêlé le vrai du faux. le film rappelle que le verdict ne coïncide pas forcément avec la vérité, et les hypothèses de la potentielle vérité restent plausible. cependant le lien avec le titre du film est très pertinent, en montrant la chute de chacun des personnages de façon disséquées. bon, en toute honnêteté je n’ai pas aimé. le fond du film est émouvant et bien recherché. MAIS, c’est lent + dialogues interminables + bcp de choses abstraites et surtout surtout surtout le film répond à rien, ça te laisse sur ta fin, c’est à toi d’interpréter et de trouver la vérité, la fin est ouverte et ne répond à aucune questions que tu te poses durant tout le film. c’est frustrant et c’est carrément ce que je n’aime pas.

texto: c’est un film très lent, avec une atmosphère étrange et de très très très très longs dialogues. c’est un infini procès, avec une embrouille interminable, qui révèle une ambiance très sombre et des personnages tous plus bizarres les uns que les autres. on comprend pas tout et c’est très compliqué d’accrocher. certains plans sont filmées de façon original, et les scènes sont vraiment longues. c’est un film chargé en émotion, avec beaucoup de secrets enfouies. au bout d’un moment ça devient vraiment interminable, des faits surgissent, des hypothèses sont conjecturées, mais c’est jamais explicitement concret. bon ok la façon dont c’est réalisé est très intéressante. par contre, j’ai carrément détesté la fin, pcq tout le long on s’attend à une réponse concrète mais le but du film c’est justement de ne donner aucune réponse, du coup c’est super frustrant. toute l’histoire on peut l’interpréter seulement par des « peut être » et jamais par de véritables faits. chacun des personnages sont intéressants, avec des points de vus différents et des façons de subir la situation différentes, mais le spectateur est à la place des jurés, donc c’est très compliqué de savoir démêlé le vrai du faux. le film rappelle que le verdict ne coïncide pas forcément avec la vérité, et les hypothèses de la potentielle vérité restent plausible. cependant le lien avec le titre du film est très pertinent, en montrant la chute de chacun des personnages de façon disséquées. bon, en toute honnêteté je n’ai pas aimé. le fond du film est émouvant et bien recherché. MAIS, c’est lent + dialogues interminables + bcp de choses abstraites et surtout surtout surtout le film répond à rien, ça te laisse sur ta fin, c’est à toi d’interpréter et de trouver la vérité, la fin est ouverte et ne répond à aucune questions que tu te poses durant tout le film. c’est frustrant et c’est carrément ce que je n’aime pas.

Para mí, la película es una mezcla entre una historia fácil de seguir y el cine de arte. texto: Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. texto: This was awesome. Might be a higher score on rewatch. I’m gonna sleep and give my full thoughts tomorrow. Best Criterion purchase I made since Memories of Murder . ________________________________________________________ Anatomy of a Fall enticed me from the premise alone. A woman is blamed for her husband’s death and the only witness is her blind son. That in it of itself is enough to get my attention. The film is an amazing courtroom drama. It’s similar to A Few Good Men in that every single court sequence is riveting, filled with incredible dialogue and tense confrontations. The movie does a great job creating suspense and tension. I genuinely did not know how it was all gonna play out. What makes this movie stand out though is at its heart, it’s a family drama. It’s about a marriage on the brink of collapse, and how the couple’s issues are impacting their loved ones. It tackles very real topics like infidelity, sexuality, childhood, abuse, depression, and grief. I found myself caring about these characters and the struggles they endured throughout the movie’s runtime. Everything about this movie felt real. Never once did I feel like I was watching a movie. Anatomy of a Fall felt more like someone hid a camera inside someone’s house rather than actors reciting lines from a script (a very well written script I might add) in front of a camera. The authenticity of this film is thanks equally to the screen writer(s) and the actors. Sandra Hüller in particular is downright incredible. The realism of this movie is a bit of a blessing and a curse. I love that the director allowed certain scenes to “breathe.” It created a bunch of heartfelt moments and it gives the viewer the chance to sit with these characters and empathize with them. That being said, I felt like some scenes dragged on for a little too long, and it ruined the pacing in some parts. But once again, maybe on second watch, I’ll feel differently. Bottom line, I love Anatomy of a Fall . I can’t wait to watch it again. In fact I kinda have to watch it again. I watched it while my wife was at book club. When she returned and realized I was watching this movie, she was like “OMG I wanted to watch that too!” Sorry babe. 😜

texto: Mettez du respect et de la lumière sur le cinéma féminin. Un film de procès qui ne cherche jamais vraiment le verdict, mais la faille. Triet construit son récit comme une dissection minutieuse du couple, où chaque certitude s'effrite à mesure que le tribunal (et le spectateur) croit avancer. Sandra Hüller y est habitée d'une opacité fascinante : on ne sait jamais si son intelligence est une armure ou un aveu. Mais au-delà du dispositif judiciaire, c'est une question bien plus vertigineuse que pose le film : connaît-on vraiment l'autre ? Son voisin, son frère, sa sœur, son ou sa compagne ? Aucune famille n'échappe aux secrets de polichinelle, à ces zones d'ombre qui persistent sans jamais être nommées. Chaque foyer a ses casseroles, ses non-dits tolérés en silence. C'est ce qui rend le film aussi dramatique que profondément humain. Il ne s'agit pas de juger un couple, mais de mesurer combien la connaissance intime de l'autre [ et de soi-même ] reste toujours partielle, négociée, parfois illusoire. Une leçon d'humilité face à la complexité des êtres. La mise en scène, souvent austère, presque clinique, épouse cette froideur alpine du chalet, comme si le décor lui-même refusait de trancher. C'est là toute l'ambiguïté du film : il ne raconte pas une mort mais l'impossibilité de connaître véritablement l'autre même après des années de vie commune. Les 2h30 pèsent par moments, notamment dans les longueurs procédurales qui, même si elles nourrissent le vertige du doute, testent aussi la patience. L'usage de l'anglais, pivot thématique plus que coquetterie, dérange certains. J'avoue que j'ai eu du mal avec ce yoyo entre les langues mais c'est à tort selon moi, tant il matérialise la distance entre les langues, les cultures, et finalement entre les personnes elles-mêmes. Une Palme d'or qui ne fait pas l'unanimité, et c'est peut-être normal. le film refuse lui-même toute unanimité sur ce qu'il raconte comme il refuse toute certitude sur ceux qu'on croit connaître. Pas le meilleur rythme mais très bon film.

texto: I love movies like this, especially the legal aspect. It’s even better when a film manages to make it feel tense and gripping. The various camera angles and shots were well executed. The plot was greatly enhanced by the atmosphere, the music, and—above all—the characters. I found the acting to be very strong; the lawyer, the mother, the son, and especially the dog all mastered their roles brilliantly. The dog deserves an award! At times during the movie, I genuinely thought the boy was blind in real life (i.e., outside the context of the film). A very convincing performance. As mentioned, the courtroom scenes were a highlight for me, and I found the ending very powerful, too. It evoked a feeling similar to the movie *The Hunt*; the viewing experience felt stark and devoid of the usual clichés. In my opinion, the ending made the most of the situation—even if that statement sounds ironic. Fortunately, the instrumental version of 50 Cent’s "P.I.M.P." was used instead of "Jolene," which had originally been planned; "P.I.M.P." fit the content perfectly.

texto: Classic? I don’t get it! I hadn’t seen this old ‘classic’ film and was looking forward to watching it. However I was left feeling disappointed. As much as I watched ready to be impressed by the storyline or the acting performances, neither really stood the test of time for me. The story line was ok, but rather straightforward, and lacked the nuance or surprise I guess I’ve come to expect from a film like this. The acting felt just a little over exaggerated, each role neither felt a good reflection on the likely behaviour of people in that position, or had the depth of performance where the actor appears to have invested real emotional energy in the task. They were performances, more what I’d expect of the stage. Of course context is everything, and the context of watching this film back in the 50’s will likely of presented to me a very different and more enjoyable proposition. Today though this film won’t live long in the memory and provides little I can recommend to others, as much as I admire James Stewart.

texto: It's a strange film... ​At first glance, the filmmakers seem to think that the heart of the matter lies in whether the wife of the murderer has been violated or not—except they don't. Justifiably so, as they themselves declare in the movie, since that would still not make the murder permissible. Then they swerve to an after-the-fact plea of temporary insanity on the thinnest of evidence. ​The attorney (Stewart) raises smokescreen after smokescreen regarding the possible rape and the murder victim's character, offering very little to substantiate their central defense claim. This, too, his very character admits. I understand exactly what the film is doing here: it is a deliberate critique of the US legal system and juries, exposing the courtroom as a cynical game where truth takes a backseat to theatrics. ​However, while I get the point, the execution feels far too clinical. Spending nearly three hours meticulously building a courtroom drama only to conclude that the entire system is fundamentally broken—and that the truth doesn't actually matter—almost invalidates the film's own narrative. If the whole process is just an empty sham, watching it play out for that long ultimately becomes uninteresting. Because of this detachment, all the characters remain mere caricatures that we never examine more than skin deep. While the filmmakers likely intended to provoke these exact moral questions, the execution is so dry that it feels like reading a well-argued college essay—intellectually sound, perhaps, but it doesn't make for an engaging film. It's a strange film...

texto: This movie is obviously sexist and dated. It could not and should not be made today with its understanding of rape and women’s autonomy. At the same time, the legal aspect of the story is the most interesting, where the characters have to justify themselves in a court of law, where their fates are determined by their ability to perform in the legal circus. The film is true to its time and enshrines many of the ideals of the 1950s while acknowledging that the world was changing (discussions of sex and sexual assault spoken about plainly—if uncomfortably—in defiance of the Hays code). The best part is hands down Duke Ellington’s score.

texto: I think i respect this film more than i actually enjoyed it, though i still did the latter. It must have been shockingly frank and transgressive against 1949's modest culture- anyone who's seen a black-and-white movie before could tell you this wasn't normal. Maybe that's why the era's exaggerated acting style distracted me more than it normally does- it's an impressively modern film, but today those modernisms serve to draw a greater contrast against its anachronisms. Still, it's a deeply nuanced and open-ended story. Never am I told how to feel about these people, never do they explain their sense of morality to the camera- I'm left on my own to feel out my own sense of right and wrong in this fictional case, and through it, the legal system at large.

texto: I was pleasantly surprised by this one, I don't know that I'd agree if someone told me it's almost three hours long in a couple of days from now, it's such a captivating film that it literally feels like it goes by in absolutely no time. I went into it expecting an unforeseen plot twist a la Witness for the Prosecution, and maybe that's exactly why I was pleasantly surprised. The film takes its story seriously and immerses you into a pool of moral quandaries that are hard to get out of precisely because of one's lack of knowledge of the truth. At the same time as it shows you the many societal obstacles there are to the believability and the respectability of women's testimonies of abuse due to social prejudice even within what is supposed to be a serious legal process, it at the same time makes you question not necessarily that the story behind it might be a complete fabrication, but that the motivations for positioning such abuse at the center of it all might actually end up contributing to the further societal incarceration of the woman at the center of it all. I can definitely see why Anatomy of a Fall takes after the name of this one, and, even if I consider that one to be an even more sofisticated version of the educated paranoia that takes over the viewer purely via the uncertainty of judicial proceedings, this is still a very respectable film, one of those everyone should see at least once in their lifetime if that makes any sense.

texto: I think this is one of the very best courtroom dramas ever put to screen. It is a complete dissection of the legal system, the people involved, the external factors, and a balance between legality and morality. A lot of films of the same genre rely on the decision of guilt or innocence to drive the narrative, but this movie is completely different. There is so much more to a case than guilt or innocence, and this movie explores it all. Court is normally presented as this place of structure, but in reality it is a game of push and pull to sway the jury to your side. It is all about theatrics to a point where the facts almost begin to take a backseat. Not only is the legal system in question, but the act itself is, as well. A case that seems so open-and-shut is never so simple. On a different note, Jimmy Stewart is Jimmy Stewart. It was an absolute pleasure to watch him play tug-of-war with George C. Scott and even Joseph Welch for almost three hours.

No big speeches, no over-the-top drama, just people talking and trying to figure out the truth. James Stewart is great, and the courtroom scenes never drag. texto: Anatomy of a Murder forms quite an intriguing investigative drama. This confidently serves up what is perhaps the most comprehensive onscreen treatment of the judicial process. Frank matter-of-fact discussion of the main subject matter must've been quite the shock back in the "squeaky-clean" times of 1959. The counselors don't beat around the bush here. They talk about sex, rape, and murder... for lack of better terms. It's striking how relevant that particular aspect rings nowadays, especially in regard to how lawyers, officers, and judicial figures speak about women in cases involving them in any capacity. While inspired by an actual case circa 1952, the film feels ahead of its time in laying out the information to the audience. Otto Preminger's patient, level-headed direction allows what could've been melodrama to instead become a true-to-life mystery... and a fascinating mental exercise. James Stewart reliably offers yet another excellent performance. It's clever how this film plays with the trusted authority type we'd expect him to fill, notably when the trial gets heated. The ensemble cast acquits themselves superbly (no pun intended). Lee Remmick treads the line between desperate wife and seductive femme like the palm of her hand. Ben Gazzarra spiritedly lends intensity and grit into his defendant, fueling the stakes in his position. George C. Scott, Orson Bean, and Joseph N. Welch steal their scenes with such vivid presence (loud or quiet). The strength of all their performances on top of an astute script already warrants a physical media purchase. Preminger takes it further by developing an absorbing style that enables the back-and-forth to be so engaging. Charm, warmth, intrigue, and crackling dialogue foster strong interest well before the defense accepts their client. The additional layer of ambiguity kept me guessing even while I was fairly certain of how the proceedings would play out. Moreover, any viewer can read each beat, detail, and revelation differently to walk away with varying conclusions, no matter the ultimate ruling. Makes for a haunting ending that leaves a silver lining of sorts. Moody cinematography bathes in the noir aesthetic and adds considerable flair to it. Fantastic framing throughout! Some shots move in the right way at the right time, whether a gradual glide or a frantic snap. Duke Ellington delivers a ritzy jazz score that's also willing to be melancholy at points. Really dug the main menu music on the Criterion DVD, which also rules when heard in its proper context. I would advise against watching this late at night, lest you become sleepy and miss a crucial moment. Its slower burn through 2 hours and 40 minutes does accurately convey how it feels to observe a trial. Your mileage will vary there. One side character's odd detour and a couple repetitive motions stall the momentum a tad. Though I can say overall the film's a far more efficient use of time than actual jury duty. After sorting through and analyzing its intricately stitched pieces, I can attest that Anatomy of a Murder stands as a classic. Viewing several of its genre peers earlier this year (from Philadelphia to Coyote vs. Acme ) may have diluted the impact for me. Nonetheless, it's an excellent picture bearing esteemed influence.

texto: I was pleasantly surprised by this one, I don't know that I'd agree if someone told me it's almost three hours long in a couple of days from now, it's such a captivating film that it literally feels like it goes by in absolutely no time. I went into it expecting an unforeseen plot twist a la Witness for the Prosecution, and maybe that's exactly why I was pleasantly surprised. The film takes its story seriously and immerses you into a pool of moral quandaries that are hard to get out of precisely because of one's lack of knowledge of the truth. At the same time as it shows you the many societal obstacles there are to the believability and the respectability of women's testimonies of abuse due to social prejudice even within what is supposed to be a serious legal process, it at the same time makes you question not necessarily that the story behind it might be a complete fabrication, but that the motivations for positioning such abuse at the center of it all might actually end up contributing to the further societal incarceration of the woman at the center of it all. I can definitely see why Anatomy of a Fall takes after the name of this one, and, even if I consider that one to be an even more sofisticated version of the educated paranoia that takes over the viewer purely via the uncertainty of judicial proceedings, this is still a very respectable film, one of those everyone should see at least once in their lifetime if that makes any sense.

It’s funny how things are told to cut out from the record but what really matters is that the jury heard what was said. Paulie knows it so well. The prosecutor was fumbling hard without everyone else on his team. Watching the whole case unfold, it just made me go justice isn’t really real. It’s ruled by narrative more than just hard evidence. It’s a bleak look. Even the judge got charmed by Paulie and his fishing hobby talk. Paulie genuinely didn’t wanna take this case and I kinda get him. It’s so much trouble especially when it’s clear that there’s a reason why the lieutenant is locked up. I super hated the questioning scene of the rape and details from Laura. It felt so humiliating. All routes of questioning lead to misogyny. It doesn’t even matter if the rape happened or not cause they already sentence her character from the way she dresses and interacts with the world. It’s the same case for Mary whose character is questioned so much that she’s forced to reveal her relationship.  There’s nothing much crazy happening in this movie but the dialogue exchange is so fast paced and keeps everything moving. Pauline’s friendship with his recovering alcoholic friend and his secretary is cute. Their next case being helping Mary out is messed up but I guess that’s a lawyer’s integrity.

exemplo: Otto Preminger é elogiado por sua direção precisa e pela forma como consegue equilibrar drama e realismo.
texto: From Duke Ellington's sizzling noir soundtrack to James Stewart's magnetically folksy demeanor, Anatomy of a Murder has the components to make a legendary motion picture. Despite the big stars, Otto Preminger, led by Wendell Mayes' rollicking screenplay, gives us something darker, critical, yet exquisitely amoral. Anatomy of a Murder does not attempt to proselytize the virtues or failures of the justice system. Instead it parses out the strategies of a defense, accounts for the varying elements relating to unpredictable human personalities and emotion, presentation of the facts and witnesses, and ultimately leads us to Platonic conclusion of how rhetorical, rather than logical, the American legal system actually is. The movie is not intended to make you feel resolved, and the lingering ambiguities remain as mysterious and subject to conjecture as Laura Manion's heeled shoe found in the trash can. Despite the somewhat dreary outlook, the movie is led by a small-town charismatic lawyer Paul Biegler, played by James Stewart, who uplifts the audience through his character's devotion and cunning. Biegler is a realist, but he's not a pessimist. Sure, he is jaded, having lost his re-election bid for district attorney, and a bit resigned, spending his time fishing and playing piano. But he is far from unmotivated. With a witty tongue and laid-back personality, he seems unshaken through most of the film, openly recognizing the weaknesses and strengths of the facts of the case and accounting for the minute factors that tarnish the supposedly fair legal process. His character, along with his steadfast secretary Maida Rutledge and barely sober but loveable Parnell McCarthy, provide a sense of light in the gray. His client, Frederick "Manny" Manion, is recalcitrant and short-tempered. Accused of murdering Barney Quill for allegedly raping his wife, his blatant jealousy and violent acts in the jail do not help the audience believe Manny was justified. Nor would it convince the jury in the film. Manny's wife Laura Manion does not help the picture: for the standards of that time, she is considered a flirty woman who wears her clothing too tight. Biegler is cognizant of how these issues can affect his case. Biegler counsels Laura to dress modestly, not necessarily because he thinks Laura's fashion has anything to do with the murder, but because he knows how this can come off to a problematic, prejudicial jury. What is most intriguing is that Biegler does not seem to care whether Manny was justified and continues to walk a thin ethical line regarding witness coaching. Biegler inveigles Manny into the irrestible impulse defense, not because it is necessarily true, but because it is the only real legal defense available. However, Biegler's sly witness preparation tactics are fire against the procesecution's fire. For example, Claude Dancer insinuates a false narrative regarding an affair between Quill and Laura, something that even if struck from the record, will not be erased from the jury's mind. The matter of rape becomes a part of deliberations, essential to the defense. But evidence, like torn panties, are hotly scrutinized in cross examinations by Dancer. Biegler's courtroom theatrics and fiery objections are matched by Dancer's intensely hostile methods, resulting in a messy, explosive trial. The movie's climax is a stroke of luck more than it is a recognition of good method. Biegler pulls a hail-mary good-faith witness, (a trope that later became common in these types of exuberant legal dramas). Biegler's only power is persuasion: persuading the judge to overcome the often arbitrary legal obstacles; persuading the witnesses to say and do the right thing; persuading the the easily emotionally manipulated jury prone to the prosecution's smokescreens. The turn at the end demonstrates how many factors can be out of your control at trial when all persuasion has been exhausted. Beigler did all he could. He could only pray thereafter. The movie, although morally gray, ends on a light note. Biegler finds Laura's heel among the rubbish, suggesting her and Manny left in a hurry before they had to pay the lawyer's fees. Manny is concretely imperfect: he's an angry, jealous, violent, dishonest person who ditches his obligations. However, it does not seem fair to have seen him behind bars for Quill's murder. The audience is prone to celebration with the defense. And ironically, Biegler is retained by Pilant to execute Quill's estate, bringing some hope that a private practice has now been established. Despite being ethically questionable as an attorney, Biegler is rewarded. I am not bothered by this. I believe Preminger intended to show, objectively, how imperfect the legal process can be. It is subject to partial authorities, discrimination, and emotional appeal. In many cases, only by pushing the limits of the practice can an attorney triumph against the odds. The boundaries between zealous advocacy and guile are blurred.

texto: Metáforas, metáforas y más metáforas... pero ¿para qué? Una película de la que se pueden sacar ríos, mares y océanos de tinta buscando interpretaciones, significados ocultos, disertaciones, tesis... Pero que, en lo práctico, no logra lo que pretende, es monótona, sumamente lenta (sin motivo alguno, porque podría entender que fuera lenta si esto concluyera en algo) e induce al espectador al sueño profundo, donde las metáforas e interpretaciones tienen mayor fuerza y peso que toda esta película junta.

texto: A vapid, underwhelming and utterly predictable "thriller". It's such a slog, which is specially offensive considering it's 2,5 hours long runtime, and, at the end of it all, there was hardly something worth building up to. It tries to be artsy with its quiet contemplative moments and its purposeful vagueness, it tries to be political with its commentary and """world-building""", but doesn't really nail any of it. The characters are implied to be full of depth and trauma, but none of it is developed, nor has any point in the end. Just a pointless 2,5 hours, that were only slightly salvaged by Steven Yeun's wonderful performance.

texto: I think I approached this film with the wrong expectations. I started watching it as a conventional mystery, and when almost nothing seemed to happen for quite a while, I found myself getting confused. Then, when the greenhouse came into the story, I realized that this was essentially Haruki Murakami’s “Barn Burning,” a story I had read a long time ago. From that point on, I shifted my perspective and watched it as a story in which ambiguity itself is the subject. The film scatters motifs such as plastic surgery, pantomime, cats, wells, and silent phone calls—things whose very existence becomes ambiguous as the point of view shifts. It leaves you feeling as though you’ve been told something profound, but in the end, I was left with an unsatisfying feeling of having been led down the garden path.

texto: القصة القصيرة «حرق الحظيرة» لهاروكي موراكامي كانت بالنسبة لي أفضل بكتير، وكافية بذاتها بما فيها من رمزية وأفكار جميلة: الشر يظهر بلا سبب واضح. والمخيف يبدو طبيعي جدًا. لا يظهر كشيطان بقرون بل يرتدي زي أنيق. والخطر موجود لكن لا يمكن إثباته. ونخلق أوهام.. ونصدقها.. ونعيش عليها. الحظائر أو البيوت البلاستيك تمثل الأشياء المهملة والبشر غير المرئيين اجتماعيًا، وأقربهم الفتاة نفسها.. ضائعة في الحياة وذاتها، تبحث عن أي يد تتعلق بها فلا تجد أحدا حقيقي، ولكن هي تجعله حقيقي ومناسب بتصديق الوهم في عقلها، ولانه كان جذاب ف صدقت. الرجل الثري يجسد فراغ الطبقة المترفة، والبطل عجز الإنسان العادي أمام شر لا يستطيع فهمه أو مواجهته. أما الفيلم فبالنسبة لي مط القصة أكثر من اللازم، وطال بلا داع وممل، والنهاية أغلقت باب التساؤلات الذي كانت القصة أجمل بتركه مفتوح.

texto: In the Burning, Jong-su the main character wants to become a writer, but he almost never writes, his life seems to have a certain emptiness, And he doesn’t seem to really pay much attention or take much agency for most of the movie. Jong su meets a girl he knew from his childhood, Hae mi, and they start spending time together until she leaves for a trip to Africa, and she asks him to watch her cat while she is away. When she returns, she isn’t alone but with a new mysterious friend named Ben. He is apparently wealthy, and his life appears much more put together, a stark contrast compared to Jong Su. After spending some time together with Ben and Hae mi, one evening, Ben reveals his odd hobby to Jong Su. After the reveal of Ben's hobby, the movie starts feeling very sinister and at times eerie. And this reveal sets off a chain of events that consume Jong Su but also for the first time give him a certain meaning, and he starts taking some action but in the process also confusing both Jong Su but also us, the viewers, and with no real explanation to any of them, the movie remains purposefully vague, and it keeps us guessing as to what has really happened and hasn’t happened, keeping the burning truth obscured by smoke. The character of Hae mi plays an important role in translating the message of the movie, and how the characters interact with her might be one of the most important parts of the whole movie. We know from certain characters that her life is a mess, but she doesn’t really let us see this, or maybe Jong-su at first just wasn’t looking hard enough (just like the viewer being focused on the mystery), not really caring about her but mostly seeing her and her body as an object. Jong-su appears helpless to the competition from Ben, while maybe also feeling resentment towards him because of their class differences. Hae mi is concerned with her life’s meaning and purpose. Ben and Jong-su are more concerned over who will have “ownership” over her. 4/5

texto: Very subtle and creeping directorial style, really it's almost unnoticeable with how naturally the story flows from start to finish. You really have to pay close attention to fully appreciate its brilliance. The film's use of natural light was awesome, the cinematography had this way of making even the most unremarkable locations aesthetically pleasing. I love how the narrative took its time establishing and really building up the characters, as it progresses, further depth is added to each of them, which kept the mystery really gripping and unpredictable. I thought the film chose the best and most satisfying path to conclude on, answering the question regarding her whereabouts would've been lame, especially after all that amazing buildup. I usually dislike these type of ending because they often feel more like the director just wasn't able to provide a satisfactory answer to the question they posed, but in this film's case it's different, it didn't feel like a cop out, but really more of a conscious choice, one that encourages a further and more in depth rewatch.

texto: I have less to say about Burning than I thought I would. Perhaps I found it too slow or cold. I wanted it to grab me with emotion or mystery or provocation, but for the most part, Burning just simmers. Of course, I think this is the point. I suppose there’s any number of themes available for examination, but I interpreted Burning to be a study in main character syndrome. Lee Jong-su is more or less idled in life. By some combination of his social class and passivity, he is unable to find his footing. So, when Hae-mi (re)enters his frame, and subsequently offers a portal into a life of privilege and agency vis-à-vis Ben, Jong-su spirals. There’s too much ambiguity over the course of the movie for it to be unintentional; yet we watch as Jong-su haphazardly rushes to solve, villainize, and intervene. But it’s too late. In time, it becomes clear that he is leaping to conclusions because the potential for his life to finally develop some meaning is too intoxicating. These ideas are potent, even emotional. For that reason alone, I can recommend Burning with ease. I wish I had loved it, but I’m glad I at least found it great.

texto: i was genuinely debating on giving this a lower rating than what i actually have in mind because of one thing: this was based on barn burning by haruki murakami, an author i truly dislike, and also inspired by a short story of the same title but written by william faulkner, a controversial author for being an "acute racist". but because this is a film review, i will have to set aside the fact murakami has an influence on this, even though it was blatantly obvious anyway (if u have read murakami, even without knowing this was inspired by his work, you'd recognize this as a nod to murakami if not, a work of his.) a film where you will have to understand four things: ambiguity, context, narratives, and perception. underrated for what it has to offer, though idk if turning two short stories into a two hour-and-48-minute film was the way to go, but yeah i see the vision

texto: cerita perlawanan kelas pekerja terhadap orang kaya yang semena-mena itu selalu berhasil membeli (tidak dalam ruang kapitalisme) saya. belum lagi kini protagonisnya beresonansi dengan saya pribadi yang sama-sama penulis novel yang belum juga debut (bedanya naskah saya sudah diterima dan dalam tahap pengeditan) yang membuat film ini terasa begitu dekat dengan saya pribadi. sebelum masuk ke filmnya sendiri, perlu diketahui saya adalah pembaca sastra jepang yang tidak terlalu suka Haruki Murakami. di novelnya yang berjudul Norwegian Wood, saya sampai harus mencorat-coret satu halaman saking terganggunya dengan adegan seksual yang sebegitu eksplisitnya. bukannya saya anti dengan penggambaran seks dalam konteks sastra, akan tetapi menggambarkannya dengan mentah dan hanya berfokus pada “tata cara mengeluarkan sperma dalam dua halaman” bukanlah sesuatu yang menarik di mata saya. seks seharusnya dapat digambarkan dengan indah dan penuh dinamika kuasa. bisa kok adegan seks itu ditulis dalam rangka menunjukan seberapa telanjang seseorang di hadapan masalah yang ia hadapi atau seberapa kuat seseorang memegang peranan orang lainnya dalam menggerakan cerita. apapun itu, ini dapat diolah menjadi sesuatu yang punya nilai tambah dalam ceritanya itu sendiri. tetapi ya mungkin kebanyakan pembaca suka-suka saja dengan sajian yang seperti ini. di film ini saya tidak menemukan itu. Hae-mi berhasil dibuat sebagai gadis yang menggerakan Jongsu di adegan seks mereka. ada dinamika kuasa yang ditaruh di sana. ditambah bayangan di dinding selagai mereka melakukan itu juga yang memberikan petunjuk tambahan di filmnya sendiri. jadi adegannya tidak serta merta jadi penambah keseksian storytelling Lee Chang-dong. cerita dijalani dengan lamban tetapi tidak membosankan karena selalu ada yang terjadi. kamera dibuat seperti pena yang meliuk, menebar prosa di mana-mana. beberapa dibiarkan tanpa dialog. beberapa kali juga tanpa suara. seru sekali, seperti melihat seorang penyair sedang berpuisi dengan intonasi serta penekanan yang pas. iya, betul. yang pas. bukan yang seperti lomba puisi tingkat kabupaten yang semua pesertanya memakai intonasi yang sama padahal puisinya berkonsep jenaka. kita disuguhkan karakter bernama Ben, seorang kaya yang nggak jelas pekerjaannya apa. kurang lebih seperti orang-orang yang kita sering lihat di pagi hari sedang joging santai dengan kacamata hitam dan earphone di telinganya, ketika kita sendiri sedang berdesak-desakan di dalam transjakarta dengan para pekerja (dan pencari kerja) lainnya. kadang saya berpikir, “mereka kerjanya apa ya?” dan pertanyaan itulah yang ditanyakan Jongsu di awal pertemuan mereka. Haemi di sini ditempatkan sebagai hiburan untuk Ben dan teman-temannya (yang saya yakin bermasalah juga). Sama seperti yang terjadi dewasa ini, di mana kalangan menengah ke bawah disawer di platform digital selama mereka menari-nari tidak jelas di depan kamera ponselnya yang berkabut. di luar tampak seperti berkarya tetapi sejatinya kita memang hanyalah boneka hiburan kala mereka bosan saja. di sinilah yang memberakan Jongsu dengan Haemi. Jongsu menyadari itu. mereka tidak pernah benar-benar peduli dengan kita, mereka cuma melihat kita lucu. seperti anak-anak kampung yang melepas sendal saat masuk mall (saya sendiri hehe) dan ditertawakan oleh anak komplek. Haemi sama seperti itu, sedangkan Jongsu tidak. kenapa? karena dia terjamah pendidikan. pernah ada ungkapan dari seorang rusia yang hobi berceloteh, “penderitaan adalah untuk mereka yang intelek nan penuh empati.”. intelektualitas dibangun dari pendidikan. tidak melulu pendidikan formal kok. Jongsu diperlihatkan sebagai seorang yang gemar membaca (uniknya tanpa ada adegan dia membaca). rumahnya dipenuhi buku-buku yang berserakan, tipikal karakter lelaki yang ditulis Haruki Murakami. ini yang membuat kepekaannya lebih tajam melihat kondisi sosial mereka. hanya saja seorang intelek tidaklah mampu berbuat apa-apa ketika di hadapannya adalah seorang raja jahat yang memiliki segalanya. bagi saya, di akhir film, dan hanya di akhir film, film ini menjadi metafiksi. adegan terakhir adalah bagaimana kita bisa terus berkhayal (untuk suatu hari kejadian) bahwa kita juga punya kuasa di hadapan mereka. seperti Jongsu yang menulis ceritanya sendiri, kita juga suatu saat dapat membalikan keadaan di mana kita tidak lagi ditindas oleh mereka. tentu jika dan hanya jika kita semua bersatu, bukan seperti saat ini, yang kota saling meninju, membiarkan para kaya raya itu berlari pagi dengan hati dan hari yang penuh ketenangan, mengetahui mereka tidak perlu tersentuh apa-apa. eat the (bad) rich, soon.

texto: Very subtle and creeping directorial style, really it's almost unnoticeable with how naturally the story flows from start to finish. You really have to pay close attention to fully appreciate its brilliance. The film's use of natural light was awesome, the cinematography had this way of making even the most unremarkable locations aesthetically pleasing. I love how the narrative took its time establishing and really building up the characters, as it progresses, further depth is added to each of them, which kept the mystery really gripping and unpredictable. I thought the film chose the best and most satisfying path to conclude on, answering the question regarding her whereabouts would've been lame, especially after all that amazing buildup. I usually dislike these type of ending because they often feel more like the director just wasn't able to provide a satisfactory answer to the question they posed, but in this film's case it's different, it didn't feel like a cop out, but really more of a conscious choice, one that encourages a further and more in depth rewatch.

texto: El pozo es una metafora de la relación? A palabras de la chica, cayó, pidio ayuda y nadie la escucho hasta que llegó el prota y la sacó. Y se enoja con él porque no recuerda el suceso. ¿Se referira la chica a que estaba en el punto más bajo de su vida y el reencontrarse con el vato le ayudo a salir del hoyo emocional en el que estaba, pero como no mostro el interes como ella hubiese querido, se molestó y por eso lo abandono? --------------------------- Creo que la historia deja las suficientes pistas para poder sacar conclusiones varias y eso me gusta. Tiene tiempo que no pensaba activamente en una pelicula. Igual le tuve un poco de mayor aprecio al diseño de produ y a las locaciones que utilizan, como las ultimas semanas vi K-dramas que normalmente son elitistas y minimalistas (en su Diseño de produ) ver lugares que se sienten habitados fue refrescante.

texto: i feel like i’m crazy. this movie is so indulgent, so exploitative, and so gratuitous. i think it’s a necessary story. pre-civil war and the arc of a freed black man as a western makes a lot of sense. tarantino was not the man who should have done it, and the tone of this film is insulting. this setting is not the one for dark comedy. people can do what they want, they can enjoy what they want, but i find this film completely irresponsible. not only do we still have a white savior in mr. schultz, but we spend the most time with a black slave owner as an antagonist. the film plays white antagonism as a joke or comedic relief, while samuel l. jackson is played like a real villain. i suppose there is an argument to be made for dicaprio, but mr. shultz defeats him, not even our black protagonist. the messaging is all over the place. it fails to comment on the lack of true power black people could ever have in this time period by being dishonest about the positions of power they are put in in this film. the other enslaved people we see, other than the people being whipped or eaten by dogs, seem peaceful and willing. i think it paints an inaccurate picture. not to mention, what good does it do to show so much violence against enslaved people? we can use it sparingly, that’s okay, but general audiences won’t understand the gravity of the violence against enslaved people when they see it within a comedy like this. “American Slavery Was Not A Sergio Leone Spaghetti Western. It Was A Holocaust. My Ancestors Are Slaves. Stolen From Africa. I Will Honor Them.“ - spike lee maybe i’m missing something. please enlighten me. but i found this to be egregious.

texto: Idk. Sometime around Inglorious Basterds Tarantino crawled way too far up his own ass and he started trying to elevate his style of airy pulpy pastiche by grounding it in these very historicized settings and trying his hand at some revisionism. I think this largely exposes his strengths and weaknesses as a filmmaker, his strengths being that he knows a lot about movies and is inspired by some of the best filmmakers and films of new Hollywood and his earnest efforts of carrying that tradition on is touching, and his weaknesses being that he’s stupid and has very close minded views of everything and has very reactionary sensibilities. Hard to muster much of my thoughts on Django specifically because all of QTs films follow the same beats and thus have the same structural flaws. But I’ll say that while there’s a lot of righteous violence and catharsis for Django against white slavers, there is equal parts gratuitous violence against black slaves used for little more than exploitative window dressing.

texto: i was really hoping i'd like this but that was just not the case for one, hated the initial white savior complex tarantino choosing to portray parts of this movie as a comedic, stylistic western is disgusting as he simultaneously included horrific scenes of violence against black characters based upon some of the most brutal events in history (yes, i know this is a shootout western but considering tarantino and his work i don't believe this was done in an attempt to replicate and represent cruelty during slavery and specifically the civil war). a lot of this was pretty much Django aurafarming with rap music playing in the background, so much so it was almost laughable to watch him shoot people in slow motion for the 5th time. pretty much just seemed like majority of the movie was exploiting tragedy, again i don't think a homage to slavery/slavery exploitation should be written by an ableist white man who thinks it's necessary to over exaggerate actual facts into this artsy context while still fundamentally revealing the horror reality; it seems mocking and demeaning cool frames and shots i'll give quentin that but overall wasn't depicting to me what i assume was supposed to be the execution

texto: As a black female adult, I’ve come to realization that I hated  this movie solely because how Quentin Tarantino portrays the  whole concept of a enslaved man became free based on a white bounty hunter and helped him kill different slave masters. The whole movie didn’t sit right with me. To be honest, as a southern black woman herself it made my blood boiled. I had to cut the movie off halfway when I saw the scene of two black man fighting to the death for their slave master as a betting deal and entertainment. I understand he was trying to get the concept of how it was back than but I felt that it was unnecessary that every sentence or dialogue was n***a this and n***a that. An a white man directing a ‘black slave movie’ showing the different trademarks of how black people was treated, punished, and abused doesn’t sit right. Basically showing it from a white point of view than black point of view. There’s a difference. I didn’t feel educated not one bit to how my ancestors were treated back than. I used to love this as kid but as I became older I realized that this movie is disrespectful towards black people and I stand by that.

texto: Wanted to rewatch to see if I was delusional in my previous assessment of this but it’s that bad. The only thing good about this film is Kerry Washington and Jamie Foxx’s performances, they were both great. The rest of this is just a heaping pile of steaming shit; its disrespect for Black Americans and their history is aggressive and distasteful, even if it wasn’t intentional. It feels exploitative and narrow scoped, as it refuses to acknowledge the class struggles of the time amongst white people in the South and follows a lot of harmful, historical fallacies of the history of slavery in the South. Quentin, do fucking better. This is better than Inglorious Basterds , but like… come one, dude.

It Was A Holocaust. My Ancestors Are Slaves. Stolen From Africa. I Will Honor Them.“ - spike lee maybe i’m missing something. please enlighten me. but i found this to be egregious.

texto: Idk. Sometime around Inglorious Basterds Tarantino crawled way too far up his own ass and he started trying to elevate his style of airy pulpy pastiche by grounding it in these very historicized settings and trying his hand at some revisionism. I think this largely exposes his strengths and weaknesses as a filmmaker, his strengths being that he knows a lot about movies and is inspired by some of the best filmmakers and films of new Hollywood and his earnest efforts of carrying that tradition on is touching, and his weaknesses being that he’s stupid and has very close minded views of everything and has very reactionary sensibilities. Hard to muster much of my thoughts on Django specifically because all of QTs films follow the same beats and thus have the same structural flaws. But I’ll say that while there’s a lot of righteous violence and catharsis for Django against white slavers, there is equal parts gratuitous violence against black slaves used for little more than exploitative window dressing.

texto: Que FILMAÇO! Meu primeiro filme do Tarantino e, cara, é tanta coisa, tantas mensagens que te pegam. Uma hora esse filme te faz sentir raiva, outra hora você ri, outra hora fica eufórico. E, nossa, quantas sensações diferentes em um filme de faroeste. Quanto a uma crítica, não vou tentar me estender muito, mas esse filme facilmente daria uns 20 parágrafos. Bom, o filme é dividido em três arcos muito bem definidos, e eu gostei bastante dessa divisão. É bem explícita a ascensão do Django, a missão para resgatar a Brunilda e, por fim, o clímax. Cada uma dessas partes é muito divertida e cheia de críticas à época da escravidão, ao tratamento dado aos negros, ao racismo e etc. Todas essas críticas são ridiculamente bem escritas e cirúrgicas, justamente por serem secas e te deixarem com raiva daquilo que está sendo mostrado (ou, pelo menos, é isso que deveria acontecer). Ao mesmo tempo, em alguns momentos você consegue rir da situação, seja pelo absurdo, seja pela graça mesmo. As atuações são estupendas. Os três atores principais roubam a cena: Jamie Foxx, Christoph Waltz e Leonardo DiCaprio. Principalmente o DiCaprio. Minha nossa, que vilão bom. Ele é acompanhado por um subvilão, interpretado pelo Samuel L. Jackson, que a todo momento consegue te deixar com raiva. Minha nossa, que raiva desse personagem. O Waltz e o Jamie Foxx também têm uma química que funciona desde o minuto 1 do filme. Os dois são muito bons juntos e conseguem carregar boa parte da história com uma naturalidade absurda. Uma coisa que achei muito interessante foi a evolução do Django. Graças ao roteiro, é perceptível o desenvolvimento dele por meio do letramento e do pensamento individual. É muito satisfatório acompanhar isso e ver como o personagem vai mudando ao longo do filme. A cena da KKK, de longe, é uma das coisas mais engraçadas do filme. É tão idiota que acaba sendo genial, e a cena termina de uma forma espetacular. Pra terminar, só apontar a única (única mesmo) coisa que não gostei: o ritmo do começo. A diferença de ritmo entre o primeiro terço do filme e o momento em que eles conhecem o personagem do DiCaprio fez com que o início demorasse um pouco pra mim. Mas talvez seja só meu cérebro derretido pelo TikTok, enfim, fica aí o comentário. Que filme maravilhoso. Fica a dica.

texto: Que FILMAÇO! Meu primeiro filme do Tarantino e, cara, é tanta coisa, tantas mensagens que te pegam. Uma hora esse filme te faz sentir raiva, outra hora você ri, outra hora fica eufórico. E, nossa, quantas sensações diferentes em um filme de faroeste. Quanto a uma crítica, não vou tentar me estender muito, mas esse filme facilmente daria uns 20 parágrafos. Bom, o filme é dividido em três arcos muito bem definidos, e eu gostei bastante dessa divisão. É bem explícita a ascensão do Django, a missão para resgatar a Brunilda e, por fim, o clímax. Cada uma dessas partes é muito divertida e cheia de críticas à época da escravidão, ao tratamento dado aos negros, ao racismo e etc. Todas essas críticas são ridiculamente bem escritas e cirúrgicas, justamente por serem secas e te deixarem com raiva daquilo que está sendo mostrado (ou, pelo menos, é isso que deveria acontecer). Ao mesmo tempo, em alguns momentos você consegue rir da situação, seja pelo absurdo, seja pela graça mesmo. As atuações são estupendas. Os três atores principais roubam a cena: Jamie Foxx, Christoph Waltz e Leonardo DiCaprio. Principalmente o DiCaprio. Minha nossa, que vilão bom. Ele é acompanhado por um subvilão, interpretado pelo Samuel L. Jackson, que a todo momento consegue te deixar com raiva. Minha nossa, que raiva desse personagem. O Waltz e o Jamie Foxx também têm uma química que funciona desde o minuto 1 do filme. Os dois são muito bons juntos e conseguem carregar boa parte da história com uma naturalidade absurda. Uma coisa que achei muito interessante foi a evolução do Django. Graças ao roteiro, é perceptível o desenvolvimento dele por meio do letramento e do pensamento individual. É muito satisfatório acompanhar isso e ver como o personagem vai mudando ao longo do filme. A cena da KKK, de longe, é uma das coisas mais engraçadas do filme. É tão idiota que acaba sendo genial, e a cena termina de uma forma espetacular. Pra terminar, só apontar a única (única mesmo) coisa que não gostei: o ritmo do começo. A diferença de ritmo entre o primeiro terço do filme e o momento em que eles conhecem o personagem do DiCaprio fez com que o início demorasse um pouco pra mim. Mas talvez seja só meu cérebro derretido pelo TikTok, enfim, fica aí o comentário. Que filme maravilhoso. Fica a dica.

J'ai jusqu'ici adoré chacun de ses films mais là...forcée de constater que j'ai pas tant aimé que ça. C'est vraiment très intéressant et intelligent, c'est une critique et une satire évidente de ce que les humains font des bombes nucléaires. On y voit le même acteur, Peter Sellers, jouer plusieurs rôles très différents pour montrer que les humains sont, malgré tout, tous assez similaires et bêtes face à un état de paranoïa, de guerre et d'égo. texto: Eu fiz algumas pesquisas e descobri que Kubrick era fascinado pela guerra, não por glorificação militar e sim expor a fragilidade e irracionalidade humana. Em Dr. Strangelove Kubrick usou sua brilhante mente para juntar guerra e sexo em uma comédia. Durante o filme acompanhamos homens incompetentes tentando manejar uma guerra como se estivessem brincando num parquinho. Esse é um ponto que me fez rir, porque a crítica de Kubrick é extremamente real. Nas guerras atuais, ainda notamos os "fetiches" de homens no comando de potências globais se divertindo com o desespero alheio. A masculinidade tóxica pode nos levar (ou já está nos levando) a um futuro ridículo. E de novo, a cinematografia é incrível! O enquadramento dos personagens é crucial para uma interpretação mais perspicaz.

texto: I finally get why people call Kubrick a genius. I’ve watched plenty of political satires, but seeing Dr. Strangelove makes it obvious how much he paved the way for this genre. The movie isn't just funny; it's terrifying. He forces you to laugh at situations that should genuinely horrify you, laying bare how absurd and dangerous human paranoia gets when it's placed in the hands of powerful people. The most depressing part is how well it holds up. We haven't learned a single thing. Unhinged leaders are still taking the wheel, making you feel like it's a matter of when the bomb drops, not if. Strangely enough, that satire movie is right at my front door. At its core, the movie shows how much of this destruction is driven by fragile male egos and sexual insecurity. General Jack D. Ripper literally starts a nuclear war because he has erectile dysfunction and blames it on a communist plot against his "precious bodily fluids." Weapons become bizarre manhood symbols, and absolute destruction is preferred over looking weak or showing emotion. Even as the world is literally ending, the men immediately pivot to Dr. Strangelove's bunker plan because it guarantees them a harem of ten women each. It’s a brutal reminder that for men in power, war is often just an ego trip, no matter the cost.

texto: Peter Sellers’ acting is amazing. I definitely got the comedy of the film, although I think it leans more toward a kind of satirical, cynical humor. As an International Relations student, I especially enjoyed how ridiculous the politicians are portrayed and how the film almost feels like a mockumentary of political decision-making. In a weird way, it actually fits quite well with how I imagine politicians might operate from a realist perspective—self-interest, power, deterrence, and everyone trying to maintain control while everything slowly falls apart. That made the film even more entertaining for me. That being said, I have to admit I was slightly concerned about the whole body-fluid thing in the movie =))) xDDDD. Overall, an enjoyable watch.

texto: Review by David Ehrlich In the end, Denis Villeneuve was all too right: Your television isn’t big enough for the scope of his “Dune,” but that’s only because this lifeless spice opera is told on such a comically massive scale that a screen of any size would struggle to contain it. Likewise, no story — let alone the misshapen first half of one — could ever hope to support the enormity of what Villeneuve tries to build over the course of these interminable 155 minutes (someone mentions that time is measured differently on Arrakis), or the sheer weight of the self-serious portent that he pounds into every shot. For all of Villeneuve’s awe-inducing vision, he loses sight of why Frank Herbert’s foundational sci-fi opus is worthy of this epic spectacle in the first place. Such are the pitfalls of making a movie so large that not even its director can see around the sets.

texto: TIFF 2021 #5 Anybody who tells you that dUnE WiLl cHaNgE cInEmA is lying to you. It's as bad as most movies that want to set up the next big franchise (or cinematic universe--Denis seems quite intent on doing that ) do as it speaks in the language of interminable exposition to set-up the next scene, and the next, and the next, until it just...ends abruptly for a sequel that will likely never happen, and a transmedial cinematic universe that will likely never blossom past the first film. It's even more frustrating when you take into consideration how *gorgeous* everything looks and sounds. Action sequences are absolutely insane, but they hold no weight to them, as the characters are walking and talking exposition machines. And they say the most ridiculous things too (the Herbert jargon isn't the problem here, though if you don't know what "gom jabbar" and "kwisatz haderach" means...good luck, but its entire script is written the exact same way as the "including my son" line from TENET brought no stakes and caused unintentional hilarity to anyone who watched the film). Yes, Dune is a highly complex book, probably one of the densest works of sci-fi there is, but there's no need to adapt Frank Herbert's work into the most uninteresting way possible. It wants to pull us into Herbert's world, yet does very little effort to actually invest us into it past its undercooked characters and exposition-laden script. FULL REVIEW

texto: Difficile de réaliser que cette expérience se termine ! Dune a pompé toute ma joie, toute mon énergie tel un vers des sables. La seule chose notablement plaisante dans ce très long-métrage est ses plans : très jolis, beaux à voir. Bien que les costumes notamment bellement réalisés permettent de se projeter dans cet univers alternatif de fiction qu'est Dune . Malgré tout, ce film fut une torture et m'a renvoyé au jour qui avait déterminé le début de ma longue période de haine envers le cinéma. Sa lenteur, son écriture, son essence n'a pas grand chose à envier à Twilight , surtout au niveau du personnage principal. Pourtant, je suis surprise de le voir reconnu de façon différente que celui-ci ! Finalement, je préfère oublier cette expérience horriblement ennuyeuse (et ennuyante) — même si cela me sera difficile.
