texto: Wow, I really don’t know what to say. Villeneuve is easily one of my favorite directors, and he creates such an expertly crafted story of family, war, and grief. The landscapes and visuals pull everything together so well, with static and lingering shots that really make you feel the emptiness and harshness of the world. It takes you through a multigenerational story, slowly unwinding the truth behind so much mystery. The first hour broke me, and I was out of tears for a while, but I assure you I would’ve had more if possible. Radiohead being the only songs in this is kinda hilarious, but it also works. As soon as the first song began I instantly recognized it and thought, “how does Denis have the audacity to play this after what just occurred.” It’s such a gruesomely real look into the world of war and how that shapes people. The narrative structure and time jumps, combined with the immense amount of travel, also help show the determination and desperation the characters have. It always gives you enough to understand and feel what’s happening without overloading you or cutting anything short. I do think the third act loses some momentum, and the ending itself is really emotionally deep but also a bit too coincidental and almost feels forced for impact. However, that really didn’t take away from the experience of watching this. It’s truly incredible and definitely something I have to rewatch. Wouldn’t be shocked if it rises to a 4.5 or even a 5.

texto: beh, diciamo uno dei racconti più emozionanti, profondi e meglio riusciti di sempre? si potrebbe. questo film racconta semplicemente come da trama, la storia di due figli, canadesi, che devono ricercare la proprie origini per volere della defunta madre, nel medio oriente. ma quello che narra il film semplicemente è un viaggio intrecciato con l'amore familiare, le atrocità della guerra e il disperato bisogno di sapere, sapere la verità sui propri cari. cioè sinceramente è abbastanza sconvolgente, riesce per tutto il film a essere e rimanere così costantemente appunto, disarmante perchè sia nelle scene di guerra, di fuga o anche solo di dialogo, si sente proprio tutto l'orrore dei personaggi che soffrono e lottano fino allo sfinimento contro tutti e tutto. poi c'è sicuramente una grande fotografia da parte di villnueve che usa benissimo il grande panorama medio-orientale per farci capire che purtroppo a volte il mondo, sceglie il destino per alcune persone come la madre dei due figli, che non ha potuto scegliere dettata sia dall'amore che dal terrore. assurdo, molto anche profondo, per i temi religiosi, etnici e familiari ecco tutto gira lì, perché tutto diventa molto più personale quando si tocca la famiglia.

texto: Esta película muestra la perspectiva de una víctima que se ve afectada simplemente por ser ella misma, por buscar la verdad y no dejarse llevar por el odio aunque se ve “obligada “ a cambiar de pensamiento, Es una película que pone la lupa la geopolítica y sobre cómo los conflictos terminan afectando a personas que, como la protagonista, no los han elegido. El hilo de la historia no comienza porque ella haya hecho algo malo, sino porque, en muchas ocasiones, no somos nosotros quienes decidimos nuestras batallas desde el principio. Poco a poco, las circunstancias nos obligan a formar parte de ellas, cuando lo único que buscábamos era una vida estable, tranquila y poder creer en algo que realmente tuviera valor.

texto: Temu Heath Ledger A pretty good summary for this film is “What if Taxi Driver and The Dark Knight had a child and it had 0 personality? Todd Phillips really tries to create a tribute to Scorsese, but as War Dogs fails to do it, so does Joker.  Todd, again is carried into mediocrity by an amazing performance by one of the greats of our generation, who wastes his talent in this. Joaquin Phoenix puts a really good performance, in my opinion not enough to win the Oscar, thats undeniable, but his performance is clearly not enough to make this film any interesting and nowhere near the performance Heath Ledger put for the real Joker. The writing of his character is also pretty pathetic, a character that has always had political/social motivations gets diminished into a depressed maniac that begins a killing spree because his mom lied to him, that is just as disrespectful as it gets. The whole film feels like a bunch of shorts put together in order to create an overall story with no continuity or direction for the most part. In general, I'd say it's an Oscar bait and a film made for spectators that aren't willing to see the deepness in films, those who just want that served in a silver plate for them, leading to it having no actual real meaning and it feeling absolutely empty. The bizarre and bloody scenes feel like they just serve one purpose, camouflaging how mediocre the rest of the film is, I guess thats another attempt to pay tribute to Taxi Driver, but Taxi Driver is fantastic even without these scenes. I really wish the film was better, because I believe Joker is one of the greatest fiction characters ever,who has been mistreated in a lot of films, ruining his potential.

Literally has the pearl necklace breaking and everything. Would have been way better if it was just a dude who killed Jimmy Fallon, or Kimmel maybe.

texto: This films manages to show, through the eyes of an outcast, how mad and sick our society is. The clown aren’t those who comes to light, accepting the label other attribute to them, but those who hide their true identity for the sake of their reputation and of their privileges. A society where everyone was born free, each one and the same measure, but where some cannot afford even the bare minimum to live with dignity, while others plan to buy a spare mansion for summer… A society where the weaker who asks for a better treatment is seen as a fool, someone to make fun of, and the mighty go on undisturbed, craving for more. ‘Joker’ is set in the ‘80, but it shows us a truth we still live nowadays: “we are all equals, but some are more equal than others”.

texto: "É impressão minha ou o mundo está ficando mais maluco?" Esse filme é simplesmente fantástico. Todd Phillips apresenta uma visão mais humana e profunda de um dos maiores inimigos do Batman. Em vez de mostrar apenas o Coringa como um psicopata que espalha o caos, acompanhamos Arthur Fleck, um homem fragilizado, solitário e constantemente desprezado pela sociedade, até sua transformação no símbolo do caos que conhecemos. Gotham é sombria, suja, violenta e decadente, uma estética que combina perfeitamente com os temas de desigualdade social, abandono e saúde mental abordados pelo filme. Joaquin Phoenix entrega uma atuação impecável, mergulhando completamente na complexidade emocional de Arthur e transitando entre fragilidade e violência. A história também mexe muito com a cabeça, lembrando Taxi Driver, com momentos desconfortáveis e situações que fazem o espectador questionar o que é real. Apesar do ritmo lento e da duração extensa, é uma experiência muito interessante. O roteiro, a cinematografia e a atmosfera são espetaculares, e o filme consegue fazer refletir sobre sanidade, realidade e a forma como a sociedade trata aqueles que são constantemente negligenciados. No fim, Coringa vai muito além de uma simples história de origem: é uma obra complexa, desconfortável e que realmente fica na cabeça depois dos créditos. Nota: 8/10

texto: I finally watched Memento and it is one of Christopher Nolan's weakest films. Firstly I like the idea of the film, it follows a man suffering from short term memory as he searches for his wife's killer and to help himself piece the puzzle together he makes use of photographs and notes to remember key details. Now this is a fresh idea and something I haven't seen before but the execution was lackluster. The story and editing of the film is non linear. The film drops us into major plot points and goes backwards a couple of moments before that point to show us the events leading up to that major story beat. My issue is how jarring this while watching because you're confused half the time. Something major happens and then you're in a completely different scene that seems unrelated. I understand fundamentally it's to have the user feel like Leonard the main character because he has short term memory loss and throughout the film finds himself in strange situations he has no recollection of being in, but for me it made the film feel disjointed and difficult to comprehend. And the film's structure doesn't help with character introductions or development because the film introduces a character that knows Leonard but as the viewer you only get context of how they met later on, which makes it difficult to understand characters' motivations and why they behave the way they do. Another issue I have are the black and white exposition dumps Leonard gives us; they are misplaced and the black and white filter feels out of place. If the purpose of the film was to make the viewer as confused as the main character I'd say Nolan did a great job. The only positives of the film are Leonard's monologues. Most of the film is spent inside Leonard's head and Guy Pierce does a great job portraying his confusion and the struggles of short term memory loss and having to rely on notes and other people which could easily manipulated which is another aspect of the film I enjoyed. As Leonard tries to find his wife's killer you notice how the notes he makes and the people he talks to are unreliable and how he has to discover the truth when he can't trust anyone or anything. I love Christopher Nolan but Memento wasn't great.

texto: Christopher Nolan’s directorial genius elevates a linear narrative into a deeply entertaining one. By placing the audience in a constant state of disorientation at the start of every scene, Nolan masterfully forces us into the same fractured mental state as Lenny, keeping us thoroughly engaged. The awe we feel each time we piece together a clue—an ability Leonard is tragically deprived of—is brilliantly executed. We also see that the protagonist is constantly cautious about whom to trust. He suspects he is being used, and while this is true, the only proof he has to back his theories is the anecdotal evidence he has gathered himself. This is a puzzle we, the audience, are also trying to figure out for the majority of the film. Towards the end, we realize that he is indeed being manipulated: by Natalie for arguably pragmatic reasons, and by Teddy, who kills two birds with one stone by giving Lenny a purpose for living while also serving his own personal interests. Because of this shared confusion, the audience is led to believe that Lenny's truth is our truth. However, at the actual chronological end of the story, Lenny subtly reveals that he’s actively choosing to live for revenge. He desperately wants meaning for his actions, or in his own words: "I have to believe in a world outside my own mind. I have to believe that my actions still have meaning, even if I can't remember them." The true tragedy is not what he has forgotten, but what he actively chooses to bury. His inability to move on is not simply because he cannot make new memories, but rather because of his own active choice to forget the ones that don't fit his narrative. Teddy captures Lenny’s state perfectly: “So you lie to yourself to be happy. Nothing wrong with that—we all do. Who cares if there's a few little things you'd rather not remember?" This perfectly reflects the true message of the film: the choices Lenny has made since the incident are ultimately to blame. His willingness to lie to himself leads him to commit terrible tragedies just so he can live comfortably in a fabricated reality. He chooses to ignore everyone's warnings and run from the truth. Despite everything that is revealed, he willfully continues living in ignorance, perfectly punctuated by Lenny's—and the film's—final line: "Now... where was I?" before looping seamlessly back to the opening sequence.

texto: This isn't as strong as some of Nolan's other works on rewatch; whereas in most of his other films, knowing where you're headed makes you appreciate it more, in this, the surprise is half the fun. The gimmick is spectacular but I can't say I gained much appreciation of this nine years later. Although I didn't quite remember all the details of the final twist, the journey there just wasn't as exciting. Still, Guy Pearce is excellent, the noir elements work perfectly, and that ending is still stellar. This honestly probably reads too harsh for the amount of enjoyment and engagement I got out of this viewing. Really need to watch the chronological cut some time; this is truly the arrival of Nolan as a filmmaker, even if it really took until he took on the Caped Crusader for him to fully gel for me. texto: Dans la catégorie des films que j’aurais jamais regardés de moi même mais que j’ai vus parce qu’ils passaient à la télé, Mother! c’est celui auquel je pense le plus. Je le prends comme un film d’auteur qui cherche à dire un truc de très vrai mais qui le fait par la recherche d’impact tellement dérangeant que ça dessert l’œuvre. Au fond, c’est l’histoire d’un écrivain qui voue sa vie à l’écriture de son livre, et qui une fois publié le regarde être disséqué, analysé, jugé par le public qui ne connaît pas la personne qui l’a écrit, seulement le produit fini. La mère qui donne naissance à son bébé, et qui invite des parfaits inconnus pour célébrer sa naissance, et les inconnus se mettent à fouiller les placards, à faire comme chez eux, et a un moment le bébé tombe par terre et les gens mangent le bébé - Stop. Y’a des trucs qu’on fait pas. On met pas en scène un bébé qui se fait dévorer par une foule de sauvages. Et pourtant, si j’en crois le film, je fais donc partie de ces gens qui piétinent sa création. Mais il y a une difference entre faire comprendre qu’on saccage sa création et montrer un nourrisson se faire déchiqueter par une foule sous les yeux de sa mère impuissante et de son père qui refuse d’agir Et à l’époque quand j’ai vu ça, ça m’a carrément énervé. Comment ça y’a un studio qui met en scène un truc comme ça et ça sort en salles et c’est acclamé par le public? On touche pas les bébés. Y’a des limites. Pour moi c’est de la branlette intellectuelle d’auteur. Si tu veux faire du sensationnel, fais confiance à ton public au lieu d’aller chercher dans un registre aussi malsain.

texto: Je trouve ça dommage de faire un huis clos pour y mettre tous les éléments de l'extérieur tels qu'ils sont. Par exemple une manif, la guerre, la police ? Dans une maison ? J'ai adoré la première partie, la tension est extrêmement forte, la mise en scène est vraiment plaisante, il y a un vrai jeu entre des plans très serrés et des plans en pdv subjectif plus larges. Ça donne une impression de voyeurisme, comme si la femme et la maison était la même personne (ce qui est le but). Ensuite il y a les premiers invités (la famille nucléaire), cette tension continue et en même temps des mystères se développent : qui sont ils ? Que se passe-t-il au sous sol ? Que signifie cette pierre ? Qu'écrit le mari ? C'est oppressant, on ne sait rien et tous les éléments sont stressants. À partir de ce moment là c'est très bien, les symboliques sont délicates, complètes et ça garde une forte puissance de propos. Personnellement j'y ai d'abord vu une idée féministe, la femme fait un travail monstrueux de rénovation pour que l'homme ait tout le buzz en écrivant (alors même qu'il écrit pas). Ensuite arrivent tout le reste de la famille, ça continue d'être stressant mais ça en devient ironique. C'est à dire qu'avant on savait que ça pouvait déraper puisqu'il y a avait un petit groupe d'intrus, mais là avec un groupe de 20 personnes, toutes différentes, la seule peur qui reste c'est la gêne qu'on ressent face à leurs comportements. Après que tout cela se calme, on revient sur du bon contenu : la relation dans le couple. Puis suite à la révélation de la grossesse et la fin de l'écriture, tout repars en couilles. Mais cette fois si c'est pire puisque plus rien n'a de symbolique. L'intérêt du début c'est surtout qu'il y a une symbolique cachée qui est la genèse de la bible. Mais passé cette étape là, on se lance dans une critique du christianisme d'une manière grossière. Pourquoi ne pas continuer le jeu de la symbolique ? Pourquoi faire des évènements aussi burlesques ? C'est vraiment de plus en plus grossier, tout ça pour avoir une critique très mid style "ah ouais la bible dit de tout partager, d'être gentil avec son prochain mais les gens ils sont pas gentils boubouuh 😣"  ou sinon une critique un peu incompréhensible qui est que Dieu ce flocko il veut trop la fame. Mouais à revoir. En plus le propos féministe que j'ai expliqué avant est bien estompé puisque ce n'est pas vraiment la femme qui charbonne (dans les 2 sens du terme) mais c'est Dieu qui crée Marie (la maison) comme hôte afin d'accueillir Jésus pendant qu'il écrit. C'est à dire qu'elle ne travaille pas vrm, c'est elle la maison et elle se prépare juste à son rôle premier : accoucher de l'autre pelo à l'auréole. Au global, le film avait un potentiel de fou, mais on ne sait pourquoi c'est passé du thriller horrifique à du comique.

texto: Very disturbing introduction to Aronofsky. This had a really strong first hour, that for me tapered off as it progressed. The atmosphere was well done, sort of established a dream-like state that made the bizarre escalation of events not seem too far fetched. Mostly felt like this was done through all of the characters interactions being very distant to mother, with an emphasis on her husband. Nobody’s really responding or registering with her actual dialogue - really isolated Lawrence as the only grounded character, super terrifying when taking into account the husband is her only lifeline in the setting and he quickly shows he is not reliable. This, as well these long panning shots of mother claustrophobically close to the camera attempting to maneuver her home (in which continuity seems to only apply where she is present) make it super nightmarish. Was super off trying to analyze this movie, first half felt more like a psyche thriller and I thought these visiting characters were representing all aspects of doubt in her life, like the man challenging her autonomy over the home and decision making while the women challenges her adequacy as a wife and potential mother - the sons would just be some internal violence I guess? Came around to the biblical allegory thing but I think my original outlook tainted the way the rest of the film panned out. Solid overall.

texto: Uma das obras mais densas que eu já vi. Tal qual experimentar um prato que de tão spicy deixa a sua boca adormecida, e mesmo assim você curte a experiência, Mother não é filme pra você sair tranquilo, é pesado, espesso, um turbilhão que te deixa cansado. Eu pessoalmente nunca fui masoquista que gosta de sofrer com algo que era pra me trazer júbilo, mas Darren Aronofsky acaba por me fazer senti prazer em ver algo pertubador. Caim, Abel, Adão, Eva, Cristo, Mãe, A humanidade, todos esses são muito bem retratados, mas estão simplesmente ofuscador por Javier Bardem, um ególatra maluco que interpreta Deus, só fica a pergunta de: como ele consegue ser tão perfeito na própria visão, e mesmo assim ser a pior coisa da existência?

texto: the track ‘dawn’ from pride and prejudice is played over the scene where josephine flashes napoleon so that was quite an experience for me i’m quite disappointed by the battles, i mean austerlitz was napoleon’s masterpiece and it barely got any screen time (and leipzig got nothing!) and waterloo…the funniest thing was when a rifleman said ‘i have bonaparte in my sights, should i shoot?’ as if firstly the french and english command tents were that close together and secondly as if you could make that shot with a baker rifle 😭 also the french having no idea what to do with square formation- where are your cannons napoleon? the entire battle was just wrong no french column advance, napoleon RIDING INTO BATTLE???, wellington commentating like its a football match what a joke there are a lot more inaccuracies, but, putting those aside, this film was boring and slow and focused far too much on bonaparte’s romantic entanglements and (inaccurately detailed) statecraft rather than his military genius and tactical brilliance and i recommend anyone who wants to watch an actual napoleonic film to watch waterloo (1970) regrettably watched the directors cut ._.

texto: Ce film aurait pu traiter des sujets passionnants : les stratégies de combat de Napoléon, sa manière d'être et de commander durant la guerre, ce qu'il cherchait réellement à obtenir. Au lieu de ça, le film se concentre presque exclusivement sur sa relation avec Joséphine, du début à la fin un choix assez insupportable, étant donné que cette relation est montrée de façon plate. Cela dit, de mémoire, le film reste visuellement correct, sans plus. La bande-son, en revanche, est vraiment réussie.

texto: Wow, making a movie this bad and disrespectful to one of history’s greatest generals must have taken some genuine effort from Ridley Scott. Half of the events are put out of order, on the wrong dates, or straight up invented in the way they played out. The actual historical beats the movie hits are given zero context, so even the stuff he gets right would mean absolutely nothing to someone who doesn’t already know the history. Every battle boils down to Napoleon ordering and leading new slo-mo cavalry charges instead of any sort of tactical genius he was known for, but at least some of the battles are were shown. Nothing is even mentioned of all the political, social, and economic reform that helped Napoleon be remembered as a great leader. Instead the decision is made to focus purely on Napoleon’s relationship with his first wife, repeatedly depicting him as a creepy, emasculated, and infantilized weirdo throughout the endless pointless scenes of them together. I was so excited when I saw the trailer for this, since It would’ve been so easy to take this cast and budget and produce an epic period piece on Napoleon. He undoubtedly had a very intriguing life that doesn’t need any imagining or changing to make into a great movie, but instead it was fucked up so bad that I could barely even finish it. So bad I just had to write this to get my share of dogging in on this movie 3 years after release

texto: ‘ France… Army… Joséphine .’ These are widely cited as the final words of Napoleon Bonaparte, encapsulating the three most important things that drove his 51 years of life. Ridley Scott’s 2023 Epic Historical Drama Napoleon feels like the culmination of two centuries of British propaganda; which reduces one of history’s most complex figures into a bumbling, pathetic character who’s only drive is his love for his wife to the point it comes off as a total mischaracterisation of the man. Despite my criticism of Napoleon’s characterisation Joaquin Phoenix’s performance is excellent and perfectly captures the character Scott intended to create. The portrayal of Napoleon as an insecure and emotionally immature man who lashes out at those around him and is only driven by having an heir to secure his imperial dynasty left me actively rooting against him at all times and sympathising with Joséphine. Vanessa Kirby’s performance of Joséphine rivals, if not overshadows that of her co-star. She brought a sense of warmth, struggle, and humanity to the screen. This makes Joséphine feel much more compelling than Napoleon and I found myself vividly enjoying her scenes; while having to suppress the fact the on-screen relationship’s historical accuracy is to be debated. Kirby’s performances was one of the only parts of the film I enjoyed as I felt it had decent emotional weight and focus compared to the other parts of the film. Scott’s attempt to encompass 22 years of the film’s namesakes’ life leads to many major moments in his military and political career are rushed through with little to no historical context or reduced to defining moments in the film created to impress and not inform. Moments such as the French Invasion of Egypt serve only to include notable monuments such as the Sphinx and the Giza Pyramids. Additionally, Napoleon’s eventual desertion of the campaign in order to attempt to seize the opportunity to gain power in the shadow of the French Revolution is instead used to further bolster the romance plot that plagues the film. Conflicts such as The Siege of Toulon , The Battle of the Three Emperors , and The Battle of Waterloo excel in being large eye-catching set-pieces with even those who are not interested in military history will find captivating. However, those who are fascinated in military history; myself included will find ourselves yelling at Scott to include what made those battles so important to the magnitude they are still studied today. I applaud Scott for attempting to create a film on one of history’s most fascinating and decisive figures; however the film fails to fulfil what an audience wishes to see in a two hour feature on Napoleon. Viewers wish to see the story of how an outsider from the Corsican gentry who was dismissed due to prejudice, uses the chaos France was in to become an Emperor. The Napoleonic Wars should have been the focal point of this film, however Scott creates an historical epic that is more focused on being a romance with hints of grandiose set-pieces with the intent to appeal to a large audience. Ultimately this leads to a film that appeals to no-one and is instead carried by the historical name associated to it and the performances of Phoenix and Kirby . As many grievances as I have with this film I would still recommend it if you are able to ignore the mischaracterisations and historical gaps. I understand that general audience may be able to ignore these due to not having enough knowledge on the time period or simply not caring, however as someone who’s always been captivated by the time period I simply could not.

texto: The year is 2023, and two new biopics have been released about some of the most destructive men known to our world. One of those films is named Oppenheimer, and it clocks in at roughly three hours and one minute. The other film is named Napoleon, and it clocks in at roughly two hours and thirty-eight minutes. Now ask yourself: Which film is longer? If you answered Oppenheimer, then you haven’t watched both films. After a rewatch the film decidedly conveys its points a lot better, and it’s a decent biopic that separates the man from the myth. That being said, decent is the word for it, because half of the time either Joaquin’s acting is meandering and aimless or Napoleon’s mood is being written to abruptly shift contradictory to how he should be acting. The one highlight of Napoleon’s writing is it at least shows the slow degradation of the main character’s mannerisms as they get overtaken by ambition. For anyone wondering, yes I have watched Oppenheimer before and yes at some point I will rewatch it and rate it accordingly. Anyways that’s it; no need to drag this review out in the way Napoleon drags out its runtime.

texto: ★★★★☆ (8/10) Napoléon est un film que j'ai beaucoup apprécié. Les scènes de bataille sont spectaculaires, la mise en scène est magnifique et les décors donnent une véritable impression de grandeur. Visuellement, le film est très impressionnant et certaines séquences restent gravées en mémoire, notamment l'entrée de Napoléon dans Moscou ou les grandes batailles. Joaquin Phoenix livre une très bonne performance et l'ensemble du casting est convaincant. J'ai aussi aimé la façon dont le film montre les différentes facettes de Napoléon, aussi bien comme stratège que comme homme. Je comprends les critiques de certains historiens sur les libertés prises avec les faits et le fait que le personnage ne soit pas toujours représenté de manière fidèle. Mais en mettant de côté l'exactitude historique, cela reste un très bon film. Je l'ai avant tout regardé comme une œuvre de cinéma, et de ce point de vue, j'ai passé un excellent moment. texto: I've always thought that making a film about a great historical figure is one of the hardest things a director can do. Unless it's a TV series or a whole film saga, trying to fit an entire life into a single movie means leaving out a lot of important moments. And when that person is Napoleon Bonaparte—a man whose life was defined by politics, military genius, and an incredibly complex personality—the challenge becomes even greater. Any filmmaker has to balance historical accuracy with cinematic spectacle, and I think Ridley Scott only partially succeeds. The film follows the major milestones of Napoleon's life in chronological order and recreates some of his most famous campaigns. At the same time, it takes several dramatic liberties to make them more visually impressive. The cannon fire aimed at the Pyramids never happened, Napoleon wasn't present at Marie Antoinette's execution, and the famous frozen lake sequence at Austerlitz is a huge exaggeration of what actually took place. Those scenes are entertaining, but they prioritize spectacle over history. Honestly, those changes don't bother me that much because they're based on real events that have simply been dramatized. What I do miss are the omissions that make it harder to understand who Napoleon really was. The film barely touches on his background as a member of the Corsican minor nobility, something that was essential in allowing him to attend military school in France and begin the career that eventually led him to become Emperor. Joséphine also deserved a more nuanced portrayal. The movie mostly reduces her role to Napoleon's wife and his desperate need for an heir. While that was certainly an important part of their relationship, she was also a politically influential figure who navigated the highest circles of French society and played a significant role while Napoleon was away. The film turns a remarkably capable historical figure into little more than a romantic subplot. That said, I do think the movie succeeds in portraying Napoleon as more than just a military genius. We see an awkward, emotionally intense man whose love for Joséphine shapes much of his personal life. Joaquin Phoenix captures that contradiction between the vulnerable individual and the unstoppable conqueror surprisingly well. I also liked how the film hints at Napoleon's admiration for Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great. At times, Scott presents him as someone driven by an almost classical sense of duty—a man convinced that his destiny was to serve France above everything else. Whether intentional or not, that echoes the Roman ideal of devotion to the state and adds another layer to his character.

texto: Un deuxième visionnage bien rentable, cette fois-ci vu en version intégrale qui rajoute 48 minutes environ. Je me rappelle que la version cinéma de 2h40 donnait l'impression que les évènements s'enchaînaient bêtement et sans raison, ce qui n'est pas le cas dans la director's cut. Napoléon de Ridley Scott est indéniablement imparfait et inégal. La photographie est parfois sublime, parfois absolument infecte. Bien sûr, c'est plus souvent beau que laid... Mais je ne peux vraiment pas passer outre cette scène d'ouverture affreuse, qui annonce vraiment mal le film. Qu'est-ce que c'est moche pendant la première minute ! La musique aussi est pompeuse pendant une bonne heure avant de devenir bonne. Mais les scènes d'action sont particulièrement réussies : très belles, toutes uniques, on comprend bien ce qui s'y passe (pas comme dans un certain blockbuster récent que je ne citerai pas...), et durent globalement le temps qu'il faut. Il faut noter que le film s'essouffle un peu pendant la deuxième heure avant de repartir de plus belle. En terme de mise en scène, c'est à la fois subtil, maîtrisé, et parfois un poil grossier/burlesque, ce qui n'est pas nécessairement un défaut. Je pense que c'est le genre de films ou beaucoup de détails nous échappent et que l'on découvre au fur et à mesure des visionnages. Ensuite évidemment, là où le film ne prend pas tellement de risques en matière de costumes et de décors (ce qui me dérange un peu car la reconstitution historique ne m'intéresse franchement pas, et je n'aime pas tellement le style de cette époque), il en prend énormément sur le fond. Et cette prise de risque fondamentale, qui est de faire de Napoléon un personnage mauvais et comique, est géniale ! Elle porte franchement le film et lui donne un intérêt. Phoenix est excellent dans ce rôle (sous certains angles, la ressemblance avec le vrai Napoléon est frappante). L'idée de faire d'un Empereur que la tradition historique prend au sérieux un simple cocu immature en manque d'amour et qui a clairement des dizaines de manques à combler, c'est merveilleux. De quoi rendre fou tout morveux qui prétend être un patriote en adorant ce neuille de Napoléon. Qu'est-ce que je préfère un protagoniste de la sorte, absolument inattendu et presque dégoûtant, à un personnage historique qui répond simplement aux attentes d'un spectateur lambda qui s'attend à un film épique comme les autres, du style Pierre Niney dans le Comte de Monte-Cristo. Bien entendu, j'aime bien Pierre Niney malgré sa filmo douteuse, mais le comparer à Phoenix c'est comme comparer une panthère et un moustique. Aussi pour revenir sur le personnage de Napoléon, j'apprécie beaucoup l'idée d'en faire un mégalo matrixé par l'envie de devenir un des grands de l'histoire au point d'écrire sa propre histoire de son vivant. (Bien sûr Napoléon de la vraie vie était aussi quelqu'un d'intelligent, à l'origine de plusieurs avancées notables, un fin stratège etc... Ok, mais dans un film c'est pas intéressant de voir ça. Je considère également qu'une grande intuition n'empêche en rien qu'il fut une grosse merde humaine). Les deux motifs sur lesquels je devrai davantage me concentrer au prochain visionnage seront la possessivité de Napoléon à l'égard de Joséphine/La France, et la lumière céleste. Bref, un film imparfait mais pour lequel j'ai étonnement développé avec le temps une réelle tendresse. Inutile de préciser que tout ce qui est vérité ou crédibilité historique est pour moins un non-argument car il s'agit de fiction, et que Ridley Scott a bien raison de se torcher le cul avec les livres d'histoire.

texto: Really was a game of two halves Or maybe a game of 3/4 and 1/4 The majority of this film was weak and not compelling in the slightest: the silence and lack of a soundtrack worked to better the atmosphere in very rare moments but most of the time it made the actions of the two leads seem mundane and boring; like the circumstances they’re in aren’t unusual at all and are in fact an every day occurrence. It made it hard for me to believe there was anything profound going on between them. The dialogue I also took issue with. The way they spoke to eachother in such plain terms and narrated every single action in a way that could MAYBE be construed as an intimate analysis between lovers. I can’t deny the acting there was beautiful and tragic.

texto: "Il faut être deux pour être drôle." Un poil trop long. Le scénario est plutôt simpliste mais bien amené, ce qui permet de s'attarder sur les émotions des personnages et de prendre le temps d'explorer les sensations. J'ai bien aimé le fait que les décors soient très épurés, même si, quelquefois, cela donne une impression d'inanimé. Surtout en ce qui concerne la pièce centrale du film : la maison. Les plans de caméra sont simples, souvent rapprochés, ce qui donne une impression de proximité, mais leur répétition amène un sentiment d'ennui. J'ai davantage apprécié les plans en extérieur, plus libres et plus fleuris. Les actrices ont une interprétation des rôles assez captivante, surtout en ce qui concerne Adele Haenel. La réussite réside dans l'expressionnisme du visage, qui dépeint une nature différente de ce qui se reflète sur la toile. Ce sujet de la peinture froide et inanimée n'a pas assez de place dans l'intrigue principale, ce qui est malheureux. Néanmoins, certaines scènes sont captivantes et nous font nous attacher à cette romance complexe et touchante. Gros coup de cœur pour le groupe de dames chanteuses et leur magnifique mélodie. À VOUS LES STUDIOS 3.28

Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019) Directed by Céline Sciamma Rating: 10 / 10 | Masterpiece ​Portrait of a Lady on Fire brought me to tears. It is a masterpiece that transcends usual romantic boundaries and clichés, burning down the traditional rules of the genre to create a love story that feels entirely, breathtakingly new. It starts on an isolated island, where a talented artist named Marianne (Noémie Merlant) is commissioned for a nearly impossible task: to paint the wedding portrait of Héloïse (Adèle Haenel), a young woman fiercely resisting her impending arranged marriage. Because Héloïse refuses to pose, Marianne must act as a walking companion by day, clandestinely stealing forbidden glances to memorize her subject's features to paint by night. What begins as a tense game of observation slowly ignites into a smoldering slow-burn of impossible yearning. As their walls crumble, the act of looking transforms into an explosive, deeply reciprocal romance with a devastatingly clear end. Director Céline Sciamma delivers something miraculous by entirely eliminating the male gaze. She actively strips away traditional power dynamics, ensuring the leads are on exact equal footing. The chemistry between Noémie Merlant and Adèle Haenel is electric; their bond, much like the portrait itself, is profoundly collaborative. But Sciamma’s boldest, most brilliant choice is the absence of a manipulative score. She packs every single frame with tangible emotion relying purely on Claire Mathon's luscious, warm cinematography and the visceral, ambient sounds of crashing waves and breathing. It is not just your love story. It explains the crushing tragedy of memory and the inevitability of loss. It brilliantly weaves in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, challenging us to understand the difference between making the "lover's choice" and the "poet's choice." Haunted by the ghost of their sizzling final farewell, the film teaches us a brutal truth: the perfect song seldom plays during our most formative moments, and the perfect person seldom enters our lives at the right time. But choosing to remember them keeps the fire blazing long after the romance ends. It is really a gorgeous, devastatingly heartbreaking, and genuinely might be one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a story that is uniquely lesbian at its core, yet its profound meditation on the sting of lost love makes it starkly, beautifully universal. The final, unbroken shot of this movie is quite simply one of the greatest endings in cinematic history. • Resonance / Impact: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Cinematography / Visuals: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Acting / Performance: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Direction: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Soundtrack / Score: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ • Plot / Storytelling: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ Final Rating: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ When you're observing me, who do you think I'm observing?

texto: What I love most is how the film tackles patriarchy without ever turning its ideas into speeches. It builds its argument through the way Marianne and Héloïse look at each other, paint each other, and gradually learn to exist as equals. Marianne first observes Héloïse in secret, treating her almost like an object to be studied and reproduced. "If you look at me, who do I look at?" Héloïse reveals that she has been learning Marianne’s gestures just as closely as Marianne has studied hers. The woman being painted has her own gaze, her own interpretation. Being seen becomes mutual, and equality begins when the observer accepts that she, too, is being observed. Consent changes the portrait in the same way. The first painting fails because it is made through secrecy and convention. Once she agrees to pose, the portrait becomes collaborative. Their love may ultimately be constrained by a patriarchal society that has already decided what Héloïse's future should look like, but the relationship itself refuses those same rules. It is built on reciprocity, consent, and recognition rather than possession. And when physical togetherness becomes impossible, art and memory preserve what society could not accommodate, not as a substitute for the life they might have shared, but as proof that it existed and permanently changed them. Patriarchy can dictate the shape of Héloïse's public life, but it cannot completely control how she loved, what she remembers, or the part of herself that survives in Marianne's art.

texto: Such an extraordinarily tender film, so slow and gentle, yet without a single second feeling wasted. One particularly striking aspect of this film is the use of silence and ambient sound. Early on this silence feels repressive, almost choking at times. Sound and music is used sparingly, but when it is present it is extremely cathartic. Waves violently breaking on the cliffs allow stolen glances, piano music welcomes brief closeness and intimacy, the thumping of cards brings shared laughter, the drone and sweet hum of the singing crowd a mutual look of tender understanding. Even in their first kiss the silence is too overpowering. However Marianne and Héloïse gradually break down that silence together until it bursts asunder, although not through violent noise, but instead a new silence, not repressive but intimate. Yet still they know that what they have must be fleeting and at times that very silence becomes suppressive, even oppressive, again. Together by the roaring waves they can be real, genuine, together. But not in the quiet false society. In a quiet moment Marianne has her look back, her last shared moment and goodbye. The storm has finally broken. The music at the end allows Héloïse a brief respite from the false life like she was told earlier it would, for her to feel and love and remember, her moments to escape from a society where they cannot be together. I am also a sucker for anything Orpheus and Eurydice related, and I believe this film to be one of the most interesting interpretations of the myth. Beautifully heartbreaking and heartbreakingly beautiful.

texto: This movie is an artistic ode to feminism and love • pure and genuine love that has no gender. With a complete absence of men throughout the film other than the last scene, it follows the beautiful story of a painter, a young woman called Hélöise, and her maid, Sofia. With building tension, emotional progression and throughout the most magnificent cinematography it portrays love at its most pure form and teaches us that it takes two to be funny. Hélöise is the lady on fire, Eyridice, and Marianne is Orpheus. It’s quite a foreshadowing, through this Ancient Greek myth, that these two women will eventually have to separate and be left only with the tender memory of each other. They were both the painters and the canvases to each other, slowly developing their emotions and interaction, creating dynamically this portrait together, the ultimate conviction of Hélöise, yet the occasion that prompted this tragic love story. And when I say tragic , I mean that these two were never meant to be together. And when it comes to the question “being free is being alone?” , the answer is no, being free is women helping women and making masterpieces like this.

texto: We did a spin-off, and I ended up with Portrait of a Lady on Fire. I went into this movie completely blind. I didn't know anything about it. The first thing that caught me was how visually appealing it is. Cinematically, I can absolutely see why people praise this movie so much. The cinematography, the framing, the performances, and the overall presentation are beautiful. The story is about two women and the relationship that develops between them. I understood what the movie was trying to say, and I could see the depth of their connection. I've also seen people call this one of the most perfect romances ever made, and some even compared its emotional impact to Titanic. But honestly, it didn't hit me that way. For me, I was watching it as a movie rather than emotionally placing myself inside the relationship. Even during the final moments, when people say the movie becomes extremely emotional, I was honestly just thinking, "How long is this going to take?" That doesn't mean I think the movie is bad. Quite the opposite. I think it's an excellent film from a cinematic perspective, and I'm glad I explored something completely different. I believe this is also my first French movie. But emotionally, it just wasn't for me. Maybe I'm simply not someone who connects strongly with romantic stories, and I've never personally experienced being in love, so perhaps that's one reason I couldn't connect with the relationship on that deeper level. 3.5/5

It starts on an isolated island, where a talented artist named Marianne (Noémie Merlant) is commissioned for a nearly impossible task: to paint the wedding portrait of Héloïse (Adèle Haenel), a young woman fiercely resisting her impending arranged marriage. Because Héloïse refuses to pose, Marianne must act as a walking companion by day, clandestinely stealing forbidden glances to memorize her subject's features to paint by night. What begins as a tense game of observation slowly ignites into a smoldering slow-burn of impossible yearning. As their walls crumble, the act of looking transforms into an explosive, deeply reciprocal romance with a devastatingly clear end. Director Céline Sciamma delivers something miraculous by entirely eliminating the male gaze. She actively strips away traditional power dynamics, ensuring the leads are on exact equal footing. The chemistry between Noémie Merlant and Adèle Haenel is electric; their bond, much like the portrait itself, is profoundly collaborative. But Sciamma’s boldest, most brilliant choice is the absence of a manipulative score. She packs every single frame with tangible emotion relying purely on Claire Mathon's luscious, warm cinematography and the visceral, ambient sounds of crashing waves and breathing. It is not just your love story. It explains the crushing tragedy of memory and the inevitability of loss. It brilliantly weaves in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, challenging us to understand the difference between making the "lover's choice" and the "poet's choice." Haunted by the ghost of their sizzling final farewell, the film teaches us a brutal truth: the perfect song seldom plays during our most formative moments, and the perfect person seldom enters our lives at the right time. But choosing to remember them keeps the fire blazing long after the romance ends. It is really a gorgeous, devastatingly heartbreaking, and genuinely might be one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a story that is uniquely lesbian at its core, yet its profound meditation on the sting of lost love makes it starkly, beautifully universal. texto: This movie is an artistic ode to feminism and love • pure and genuine love that has no gender. With a complete absence of men throughout the film other than the last scene, it follows the beautiful story of a painter, a young woman called Hélöise, and her maid, Sofia. With building tension, emotional progression and throughout the most magnificent cinematography it portrays love at its most pure form and teaches us that it takes two to be funny. Hélöise is the lady on fire, Eyridice, and Marianne is Orpheus. It’s quite a foreshadowing, through this Ancient Greek myth, that these two women will eventually have to separate and be left only with the tender memory of each other. They were both the painters and the canvases to each other, slowly developing their emotions and interaction, creating dynamically this portrait together, the ultimate conviction of Hélöise, yet the occasion that prompted this tragic love story. And when I say tragic , I mean that these two were never meant to be together. And when it comes to the question “being free is being alone?” , the answer is no, being free is women helping women and making masterpieces like this.

texto: Such an extraordinarily tender film, so slow and gentle, yet without a single second feeling wasted. One particularly striking aspect of this film is the use of silence and ambient sound. Early on this silence feels repressive, almost choking at times. Sound and music is used sparingly, but when it is present it is extremely cathartic. Waves violently breaking on the cliffs allow stolen glances, piano music welcomes brief closeness and intimacy, the thumping of cards brings shared laughter, the drone and sweet hum of the singing crowd a mutual look of tender understanding. Even in their first kiss the silence is too overpowering. However Marianne and Héloïse gradually break down that silence together until it bursts asunder, although not through violent noise, but instead a new silence, not repressive but intimate. Yet still they know that what they have must be fleeting and at times that very silence becomes suppressive, even oppressive, again. Together by the roaring waves they can be real, genuine, together. But not in the quiet false society. In a quiet moment Marianne has her look back, her last shared moment and goodbye. The storm has finally broken. The music at the end allows Héloïse a brief respite from the false life like she was told earlier it would, for her to feel and love and remember, her moments to escape from a society where they cannot be together. I am also a sucker for anything Orpheus and Eurydice related, and I believe this film to be one of the most interesting interpretations of the myth. Beautifully heartbreaking and heartbreakingly beautiful.

texto: Another one for psych class. This is one of the worst films I've ever seen. The performances are mediocre, with DiCaprio's likely being the worst. The writing is incredibly juvenile, even with the plausible theory that the majority of the dialogue is filtered through the guy's warped mind. The film doesn't even look good or have an interesting aesthetic. The twist falls apart because it requires you to empathize with DiCaprio's character in the beginning, which I did not. Now, to the big problems. This film's portrayal of the mentally ill is disgusting. I understand that the facility is specifically meant to house people who've committed a violent crime, but the film was arguably still irresponsible in its perpetuation of the stereotype that all people with mental illness are scary, violent, completely irrational, and are deserving of no empathy whatsoever. There is no mention of the specific diagnosis that any patient, let alone the main character, has, which makes it impossible to understand the accuracy of the portrayals. This film was made too recently to still exhibit such an under-researched and outdated parody of what a real group of underprivileged people is like. Let's move on to another problem, the film's portrayal of both the Holocaust and the implications of Project MKUltra during the Cold War. These were both serious tragedies that I feel were not handled with appropriate sensitivity and were rather just half-baked elements seemingly thrown in for added novelty. With this film exhibiting these two themes in addition to its portrayal of extreme psychosis, there are too many things being explored and none of them are done properly. The main conspiracy is clearly supposed to be MKUltra, something that really did victimize psychiatric patients during the Cold War, and yet in the movie's cannon, it's confirmed to not be happening. I don't think this film is intentionally trying to say that MKUltra didn't happen, but it's a very strange and poorly thought-out choice that is completely at odds with the setting. This movie clearly did not have anything to say about any of the incredibly serious topics it includes, and thus has no comprehensive or unique thesis. It's an offensive, confused mess that frankly has no merit as a piece of art.

texto: entretenida pelicula e interesante final, pero todo el aspecto “psicológico” de la pelicula lo senti muy cliche que me arruino el resto. muy fantástico para sentirlo real. sobretodo de personajes que deberian aterrizar los conceptos psicológicos. solo hacen que la pelicula se sienta mas como un “esto es lo que creemos que las condiciones psicológicas son en hollywood”. me saca de la inmersion y no pude evitar reirme. 5 estrellas si tuviera 14-16 años. muy dramatizado y caracterizado hasta sentirse holllywoodense, pero puede hacerse un espacio a la discusión teniendo en cuenta el cine noir, la pelicula no falla en hacer homenaje a los thrillers característicos de la epoca de estos, pero si senti que era muy “en tu cara”. no que no sea una peli entrete de ver. english: Entertaining movie with an interesting ending, but the entire “psychological” aspect of the film felt very cliché to me, and it ruined the rest. It was too fantastical to feel realistic, especially coming from characters who are supposed to ground these psychological concepts. They only make the movie feel more like “this is what we think psychological conditions are in Hollywood.” It took me out of the immersion, and I couldn’t help but laugh. 5 stars if I was 14-16 years old. Very dramatized and characterized to the point of feeling overly Hollywood-like, but it can still have a place for discussion when considering film noir. The movie does not fail to pay homage to the characteristic thrillers of that era, but I felt it was very “in your face.” not to say it was a fun movie to watch.

texto: Shutter Island is a psychological thriller film directed by Martin Scorsese and released in 2010. The movie stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Teddy Daniels, a U.S. Marshal who travels to a mysterious island with his partner, Chuck Aule, to investigate the disappearance of a patient from a psychiatric hospital. As Teddy investigates, strange events begin to happen, and he starts to question the hospital, the doctors, and even his own memories. The story becomes more mysterious and confusing as Teddy discovers that the island is hiding a dark secret. One of the best things about Shutter Island is its atmosphere. The dark setting, suspenseful music, and confusing events create a feeling of fear and mystery. Leonardo DiCaprio also gives a very strong performance as Teddy. The ending is one of the most surprising parts of the movie because it changes the way we understand the whole story. Overall, Shutter Island is an interesting and suspenseful movie that makes the audience think about reality, memory, and guilt. I would recommend it to people who enjoy psychological mystery films.

texto: "You have to let her go" "I can't!" "Then you'll never get off this island..." Enjoyed this more on rewatch, I was better able to appreciate how the mood of the island is developed, with the soundscape being particularly impressive, with original score, licensed music, and classical music all coming together really well. Weather is also used particularly effectively to make the island feel isolating and uncomfortable; there's something about heavy rain at night that makes me really uncomfortable and I love the way that is used in this film. The star segment here is Ward C, feeling like walking into a nightmare within an already dreadful environment - it feels like those segments in Silent Hill when you go from normal world to Otherworld, everything just gets so suddenly worse and terrifying with no end in sight. Despite this being a psychological thriller with heavy emphasis on its ending, it still does very little for me compared to the build up on the island (which I really enjoyed) and other films in the ending-heavy "genre" (Memento, Prestige, Fight Club, Total Recall, etc.). It just never feels like the reveals that happen meaningfully impact or re-contextualize the earlier scenes of the film. Of course the context does literally change but it doesn't really change the emotional impacts, at least for me

texto: Absolutely fantastic. Shutter Island is the kind of movie that gets better the more you think about it. The atmosphere is incredibly dark and unsettling, and Scorsese does an amazing job slowly building this feeling that something is seriously wrong without giving everything away. Leonardo DiCaprio is phenomenal here, carrying the entire movie with a performance that feels increasingly desperate and unhinged as the story progresses. The mystery constantly keeps you questioning what’s real and what isn’t, and the ending completely changes the way you look at everything that came before it. The cinematography, score, performances, and psychological tension all come together perfectly. It’s one of those movies where you immediately want to go back and watch it again just to catch everything you missed the first time. Fantastic

As Teddy investigates, strange events begin to happen, and he starts to question the hospital, the doctors, and even his own memories. The story becomes more mysterious and confusing as Teddy discovers that the island is hiding a dark secret. One of the best things about Shutter Island is its atmosphere. The dark setting, suspenseful music, and confusing events create a feeling of fear and mystery. Leonardo DiCaprio also gives a very strong performance as Teddy. The ending is one of the most surprising parts of the movie because it changes the way we understand the whole story. Overall, Shutter Island is an interesting and suspenseful movie that makes the audience think about reality, memory, and guilt. I would recommend it to people who enjoy psychological mystery films.

texto: Absolutely fantastic. Shutter Island is the kind of movie that gets better the more you think about it. The atmosphere is incredibly dark and unsettling, and Scorsese does an amazing job slowly building this feeling that something is seriously wrong without giving everything away. Leonardo DiCaprio is phenomenal here, carrying the entire movie with a performance that feels increasingly desperate and unhinged as the story progresses. The mystery constantly keeps you questioning what’s real and what isn’t, and the ending completely changes the way you look at everything that came before it. The cinematography, score, performances, and psychological tension all come together perfectly. It’s one of those movies where you immediately want to go back and watch it again just to catch everything you missed the first time. Fantastic

texto: I personally think it is a psychedelic paranoid masterpiece that is a wonderful examination of the brain, trauma, and crisis of identity. All themes which Scorsese has used before for his movies. The film is creepy, beautifully shot, extremely well acted, and leaves you in suspense until the end. While it may not break new ground the way Taxi Driver, Mean Streets, and Goodfellas do, it is one of the most beautifully shot films I’ve ever seen, and I find it quite emotionally impactful. So why do you think Shutter Island hasn’t aged as well as his other works? Even Scorsese himself said he regrets being attached to it, and I think that’s wrong because it shows just how versatile the guy is. He can direct any genre to perfection.

texto: "You have to let her go" "I can't!" "Then you'll never get off this island..." Enjoyed this more on rewatch, I was better able to appreciate how the mood of the island is developed, with the soundscape being particularly impressive, with original score, licensed music, and classical music all coming together really well. Weather is also used particularly effectively to make the island feel isolating and uncomfortable; there's something about heavy rain at night that makes me really uncomfortable and I love the way that is used in this film. The star segment here is Ward C, feeling like walking into a nightmare within an already dreadful environment - it feels like those segments in Silent Hill when you go from normal world to Otherworld, everything just gets so suddenly worse and terrifying with no end in sight. Despite this being a psychological thriller with heavy emphasis on its ending, it still does very little for me compared to the build up on the island (which I really enjoyed) and other films in the ending-heavy "genre" (Memento, Prestige, Fight Club, Total Recall, etc.). It just never feels like the reveals that happen meaningfully impact or re-contextualize the earlier scenes of the film. Of course the context does literally change but it doesn't really change the emotional impacts, at least for me

texto: 50 Across the Spider-Verse is a film that promises everything and delivers... some of it. The multiverse concept, inherently thrilling on paper, remains the franchise's greatest asset. The sheer variety of Spider-People is a joy to behold. The film does not disappoint in its ambition. Yet for all its formal brilliance, Across the Spider-Verse stumbles badly in its handling of tone, and nowhere is this more evident than in its villain. His early appearances are played purely for laughs, and while the film eventually attempts to pivot toward genuine menace, the damage is already done. He becomes a symbol of the film's broader comedic excess: the relentless quipping and meta-references that undercut every moment of tension. By the time The Spot transforms into a world-ending threat, we cannot take him seriously because the film never taught us how. The film's incessant needle drops compound the problem, each licensed track feeling less like organic storytelling and more like a calculated monetization strategy. The soundtrack is curated not to serve the narrative but to populate Spotify playlists, a transparent effort to generate revenue streams beyond the box office. This commercial calculation extends beyond the music. The cliffhanger ending? It is difficult not to view it as a deliberate fragmentation, a way to stretch a single story across multiple releases and maximize returns. What emerges is not a complete story but a dazzlingly packaged installment, one that too often feels engineered for the franchise rather than the narrative. 🕷️Homecoming Review🕷️ 🕸️Far From Home Review🕸️ 🦇The Dark Knight Review🦇 🕷️No Way Home Review🕷️ 🕸️Spider-Man Review🕸️ 🕷️Spider-Man 2 Review🕷️ 🕸️Into the Spider-Verse Review🕸️

texto: Really wanted to like this one more than I did. After all, what better way to complete my Trolls Remorse arc than giving a favorable score to the Other Miles Morales movie. Sadly, this is a textbook case of chief creatives whose eyes are far, far bigger than their stomachs. The worst of the post Gunn, post Waititi “Comic Book Authenticity” is depicted here, and this time I truly do not believe that any of the 3 writers have any kind of fondness for the comics. The focus of Across the Spider-Verse is selling moviegoers on the importance of Spider-Man as a brand within Marvel, with a set of rules to be followed; a checklist of inciting traumas to be applied where the end result is a new Spider-Man. Conveniently, the film makes this subtext text by centering the film around the prevention of “Canon Events”, tragic deaths of loved ones that must happen because That’s Spider-Man. Mercifully, Lord and Miller rarely show our massive cast experience or be changed by said traumas — a film that thinks for itself, what a Marvel. Having read more comics than I think 99% of Letterboxd, Alternate Universe stories are among some of the laziest writing one can choose. The superior first film largely uses it for Family Guy cutaway tier gags; “Hey remember the Spider-Man Popsicle” novelty signaling to the adults in the room that this is Growing the Brand but fun. Now we must succumb to the Elseworlds Comic Story Effect: writing essentially a re-themed take on the platonic Spider Man second outing, each moment signposted through overt “meta” staging, and a complete wet fart of a 15 minute 3rd act after a 70 minute 1st to boot. One would hope that character could carry us through a lackluster script, but Lord and Miller and The Other One opt for a thin but wide approach instead. It feels as if character attributes were chosen at complete random. Jessica Drew is a strong black woman working while pregnant because… Ben Reilly is brooding because the 90s were grim and dark (yet nothing in the handful of Ben Reilly appearances I’ve read would even touch the vicinity of brooding). Like the aforementioned Cutaway Gags, characters who could be Sneakers O’Toolesian delightful non sequiturs overstay their welcome and confuse. The hired gun Lego commercial got an earnest laugh out of me, everything in the set pieces to follow would not. Once again the thankless job of creating something worth writing paragraphs about falls to the Animators. Eyes and stomachs in perfect alignment, they truly deliver on great leaps forward in mainstream animation. No minced words about it: this film can look gorgeous . However, due to the complete dearth of imagination from the top down everything feels off. I found myself getting genuinely overstimulated by the film at times; nothing moves right, scenes feel poorly timed, and not a single moment felt as effortlessly evocative as the sequence in the first film where Miles leaps off a building into a colorful void. Around the 50 minute mark, as we wind down on the prologue, Across starts to look legitimately ugly. Chromatic blurs fill the screen for no other reason than to exist, the camera rapidly adjusts itself throughout a scene, and your eyes struggle to find a place to rest while taking in the composition. Very few of the colorful compositions have meaning, I struggle to ascribe any real meaning to heavy decisions like a Trans Reading for Gwen because of how arbitrary the movie can look; the curtains are simply blue. It is creative flailing, masquerading as vision. People with little experience in either often call comics and film sister mediums. Both deal in the marriage of language and visual, and storyboarding kinda feels like a comic to the layman. The analogy can be allowed to continue to live regarding Across the Spider-Verse because the disconnect between animator and Director/Writer/Producer feels as if they couldn’t be any further apart — as if the worst instincts of American comics is a style to be worshipped and imitated. If you’ve ever read a bad comic with good art you’ll understand what I mean. If you haven’t, you can buy Kingdom Come for like 10 bucks now.

texto: Au moins aussi acclamé à sa sortie, ce second opus a le mérite d'être divertissant, mais à l'inverse du premier qui était une montée en puissance sur tous les plans, plus les enjeux multiversels prennent du poids, et moins il convainc. Spider-Man : Across the Spider-Verse est bien meilleur lorsqu'il se concentre sur l'intime, même s'il demeure à ce sujet très classique. D'ailleurs, j'ai bien cru que je le préférerais à en juger par son introduction, plus aboutie que celle du précédent, mais la suite m'a déçu. Il est très frustrant de regarder une œuvre qui s'étend sur autant de temps pour ne pas avoir le droit à une vraie fin, fut-elle ouverte. Sur le plan visuel, on est dans la continuité, avec un peu plus de variété issue de l'exploration du multivers. Toutefois, je regrette l'inclusion de live action qui me sort totalement du film. Ponctuellement, certains plans continuent de me gêner par leur façon de trancher avec d'autres mais je dois dire que cela a moins été le cas qu'auparavant. C'est peut-être une question d'habitude, mais je pense surtout que celui-ci est techniquement plus abouti. Quoi que je sois critique, cela reste à des années lumières des bouses super-heroïques que nous sert Marvel à son habitude. Le moment est plaisant mais hormis toute la séquence où Gwen et Miles se retrouvent puis papotent en se collant sur les bâtiments — qui est superbe — je ne sais pas si j'en retiendrais grand chose sur le long terme. En fait, je me rends bien compte que toutes mes scènes préférées sont dans le premier acte. Après, comme c'est une expérience formelle, je suppose qu'il a l'avantage de bien se revoir. La sortie de la suite sera l'occassion de le réévaluer.

Yet for all its formal brilliance, Across the Spider-Verse stumbles badly in its handling of tone, and nowhere is this more evident than in its villain. His early appearances are played purely for laughs, and while the film eventually attempts to pivot toward genuine menace, the damage is already done. He becomes a symbol of the film's broader comedic excess: the relentless quipping and meta-references that undercut every moment of tension. By the time The Spot transforms into a world-ending threat, we cannot take him seriously because the film never taught us how. The film's incessant needle drops compound the problem, each licensed track feeling less like organic storytelling and more like a calculated monetization strategy. The soundtrack is curated not to serve the narrative but to populate Spotify playlists, a transparent effort to generate revenue streams beyond the box office. This commercial calculation extends beyond the music. The cliffhanger ending? It is difficult not to view it as a deliberate fragmentation, a way to stretch a single story across multiple releases and maximize returns. What emerges is not a complete story but a dazzlingly packaged installment, one that too often feels engineered for the franchise rather than the narrative. 🕷️Homecoming Review🕷️ 🕸️Far From Home Review🕸️ 🦇The Dark Knight Review🦇 🕷️No Way Home Review🕷️ 🕸️Spider-Man Review🕸️ 🕷️Spider-Man 2 Review🕷️ 🕸️Into the Spider-Verse Review🕸️

texto: I do not envy anyone given the task of following Into the Spider-Verse. That film singularly injected so much new life and artistic innovation into an IP that was beginning to get stagnant. It took the time and consideration to acknowledge the foundation and rich history baked into the character of Spider-Man and gave it a loving sendoff before turning to a brand new chapter. Regrettably, Across the Spider-Verse feels like one step forward, two steps back. If there’s one thing my journey through the MCU has taught me, it’s that the multiverse fucking sucks. And I understand that’s a contentious position to hold against a series called “the Spider-Verse,” but hear me out. Into the Spider-Verse used the concept in the most effective way: minimalistic. The multiverse purely acted as the inciting incident for Miles’ story, much like time travel in the first Terminator movie. Yes, you had cheeky references to established Spider-Man iterations, their tropes and standing in pop culture, but ultimately it was a measuring stick to hold up to Miles’ own hero’s journey. A narrative device showing how the character inspired this new hero, much like he has countless others in our own world. Comparatively, Across the Spider-Verse becomes overindulgent, languishing in its multiverse setting and using it as an excuse to showcase the less popular Spider-Man content, or ride the coattails of the more popular content. Remember Andrew Garfield Spider-Man? Look, there he is! And Toby McGuire! Look, this multiversal Spider-Man agency knows about what Dr. Strange was doing! And the dimension-hopping films? He talks to Mrs. Chen, from our hit Venom film series! The SPUM-C is alive and well. And look, there’s Donald Glover as Prowler! Like he was gonna be in the MCU! There’s also an attempt to make each dimension extremely unique, which unfortunately comes across like a more obnoxious attempt to copy the uniqueness of Into the Spider-Verse’s art style, and the clashing artstyles tend to make it look like a big, muddled mess. Really, with a concept like the multiverse, the last thing you want to do is get technical. Where Deadpool & Wolverine had the braindead concept of an anchor being, Across the Spider-Verse presents the “canon events.” (Which felt like such a dumb attempt at meta, I threw up in my mouth a little bit.) Rather than the shared trauma being a bonding point between the different iterations of Spider-Man, it’s now an absolute event necessary for their journey, whose disruption could lead to the disintegration of their reality. Delving more into the multiverse also takes the wind out of the sails for Miles’ own character arc. Spoilers: we find out that he wasn’t meant to become Spider-Man, as the spider that bit him came from another dimension. So he is an anomaly, and his arc is that, even though it wasn’t his destiny…he is still Spider-Man. Because he chooses to be. Which isn’t nothing , but feels like a much more hollow echo of his arc in the first film. My own cynicism and hangups notwithstanding, Across the Spider-Verse is a fine film. A far fall from its predecessor, but if you’ve been missing the characters and world, it does feel like a welcome return. It’s overbloated, and its standing as a definitive “part one” further lessens its value on its own, but it’s ultimately competent enough.

texto: Man, I really wanted to like this movie more, I loved the first movie. And make no mistake, the first two thirds of this sequel were everything I'd hoped for, gorgeous animation and art style as expected, an interesting plot with a hilarious villain who unexpectedly goes through development into a more dangerous, malevolent foe. And the sheer amount of non-intrusive cameos when they arrive at Spider City, and Oscar Isaac's performance! But with the third act everything just... falls apart. All sense of momentum stops dead in its tracks. The bad guy fails to fulfill the menace and character growth he'd promised, because the movie never actually gets that far. What should be an exciting climax instead wastes time with useless drama and a misdirection that doesn't actually add anything to plot or character, but rather just bloats out the runtime to a level Eternals would have been proud of. And then.... "To Be Continued...... in Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse!" Uh.... okay. Sure. Cut out the third act of a film, the most important part of any movie where all the tension and drama pays off, and then relegate to a sequel which will likely not arrive for years to come. And instead of an alternate climax, just fill out the last 40 minutes with mind-numbingly boring and unsatisfactory screentime. Man, what a disappointment.

A narrative device showing how the character inspired this new hero, much like he has countless others in our own world. Comparatively, Across the Spider-Verse becomes overindulgent, languishing in its multiverse setting and using it as an excuse to showcase the less popular Spider-Man content, or ride the coattails of the more popular content. Remember Andrew Garfield Spider-Man? Look, there he is! And Toby McGuire! Look, this multiversal Spider-Man agency knows about what Dr. Strange was doing! And the dimension-hopping films? He talks to Mrs. Chen, from our hit Venom film series! The SPUM-C is alive and well. And look, there’s Donald Glover as Prowler! Like he was gonna be in the MCU! There’s also an attempt to make each dimension extremely unique, which unfortunately comes across like a more obnoxious attempt to copy the uniqueness of Into the Spider-Verse’s art style, and the clashing artstyles tend to make it look like a big, muddled mess. Really, with a concept like the multiverse, the last thing you want to do is get technical. Where Deadpool & Wolverine had the braindead concept of an anchor being, Across the Spider-Verse presents the “canon events.” (Which felt like such a dumb attempt at meta, I threw up in my mouth a little bit.) Rather than the shared trauma being a bonding point between the different iterations of Spider-Man, it’s now an absolute event necessary for their journey, whose disruption could lead to the disintegration of their reality. Delving more into the multiverse also takes the wind out of the sails for Miles’ own character arc. Spoilers: we find out that he wasn’t meant to become Spider-Man, as the spider that bit him came from another dimension. So he is an anomaly, and his arc is that, even though it wasn’t his destiny…he is still Spider-Man. Because he chooses to be. Which isn’t nothing , but feels like a much more hollow echo of his arc in the first film. My own cynicism and hangups notwithstanding, Across the Spider-Verse is a fine film. A far fall from its predecessor, but if you’ve been missing the characters and world, it does feel like a welcome return. It’s overbloated, and its standing as a definitive “part one” further lessens its value on its own, but it’s ultimately competent enough.

texto: This film was a no-fun labor to watch. Only gave it 2 stars for the performances by some of the actors. First, the narrative is all over the place. It's not anti-war, it's not pro-freedom fighters, it's just ambiguous. Shot like documentary and news footage half of the time, and it still seems like an exaggerated narrative, towards what goal? Not sure really. Both sides kill civilians because of reasons. Everyone sucks. But if the whole "war=bad" narrative was the goal, Paths of Glory did it much better 9 years earlier. None of the characters were likeable, none had enough development to really understand or even care about. All were cold emotionally and dehumanized. Even if you were looking for a "fair" way to describe both sides being bad, this movie did a poor job of it. Film quality was terrible, cinematography wasn't great, even for its era. 2001 came just 2 years after this and looked like it's from another century. I watched better, lower budget documentary films from modern wars like the Syrian Civil War or the Afghanistan War that were far more compelling and up to date with modern filming quality. I just don't get the hype. This genuinely was a bore and a chore to watch.
