texto: A pesar de que me pareció un poco aburrida, considero que hay diversos puntos interesantes en esta película: En primer lugar, como funcionan las dinámicas de poder. Para empezar, toda la relación de Val con su jefa y como a la dueña del hogar no le terminaba de caer bien Val. Se demostraba en cómo le hablaba, y más aún cuando llegó Jessica, ya que se mostraba menos sumisa a Val y la jefa parecía que pensaba que era inferior a ella. Un poco en relación a esto, también como los hombres piensan que tienen poder o derechos sobre una mujer por tener una "posición" y demás. Esto se demostraba con todo el tema de que Carlos se enamora de Jessica, hasta el punto de pedirle matrimonio, cuando ella nunca le dio indicios de que gustaba de él. Por otra parte, y un poco asociado a las relaciones de poder, se demuestra mucho la meritocracia. Val pensaba que ella no merecía ciertas cosas, como el helado, sentarse con sus jefes, estar en la piscina, y le intentaba instaurar este pensamiento a Jessica, pero ella no se dejaba. También, me pareció un poco interesante que Val se interesó en pasar más tiempo con Jessica cuando se dio cuenta que tenía un hijo. Lowkey lo asocié en que ella vio en el Jorge la oportunidad de cuidar y pasar tiempo con otro Fabinho. En general, siento que toca temas sociales bastante interesantes, sin embargo, la película me parecía un poco lenta y la trama/storytelling un poco aburrido.

texto: Anna Muylaert transforma a casa de classe média em um campo de batalha silencioso, onde as paredes carregam as marcas invisíveis de quem serve. Regina Casé faz de Val uma presença que pulsa mesmo quando em silêncio, equilibrando afeto, submissão e culpa com uma naturalidade absurda. A chegada de Jéssica é o estilhaço: a piscina, o quarto de hóspedes, a mesa da cozinha, tudo vira território de disputa. O filme fala de um país que trata o afeto como salário e a maternidade como ausência. O final na porta de casa é um grito abafado de liberdade. Um dos filmes mais necessários do cinema brasileiro. 🇧🇷🏊‍♀️💔

texto: Les 5 premières minutes on se dit wow ça va être quelque chose puis au bout de 15 on se dit ah ouais ok ça va être quelque chose de sacrément long. Les gros plans sur le moindre détail hyper esthétisé et sur-symbolique, le montage net et hyper rythmé qui repose sur la cassure et la surprise de l’enchaînement des plans et des champs-contre-champs contre indicatifs, les bruits exorbitants pour la moindre chose du quotidien, la bande son sans arrêt qui se veut efficace et sans discontinuité. texto: La serie Z que rezuma. Sobre pinchazos y borbotones. Ya lo escribió Baruch Spinoza en su momento: nadie sabe lo que puede un cuerpo. Transcurrida una hora, me planteo si lo que estoy viendo es una película falsamente subversiva que parte de una idea explícita (la crítica a la sobreexposición del cuerpo femenino en la era del consumo, convertido en producto de carnicería a causa de la tiranía de la belleza) y la lleva al paroxismo. Sin embargo, conforme el relato avanza nos vamos encontrando con una suerte de retorno del espectro de "El hombre elefante", de "Carrie", de "Alien" y de otras múltiples tradiciones del cine norteamericano. Es contundente y celebratoria en el rumbo que toma y también divertida, e incluye una jocosa referencia a "Vertigo".

texto: To put things briefly, The Substance is a relatively sound film, although, it still comes with a fair share of issues. As films of this more thematic nature, and more broadly within the horror genre typically demand, you’re sort of supposed to just go with the plot, which I struggle with. It’s not necessarily poorly written, it’s just contrived, not implausibly, but I still feel the beats could’ve been better strung together. Speaking of themes, it touches primarily on our contemporary culture, our media, and on the treatment of women, particularly within the public sphere; although I do find that the film fails to boldly challenge our perception of these social facets, or issues. For example, the premise, alongside how the film is shot evidently wish to discuss the self-objectification of the individual, of which is intrinsically tied to social norms, and to capitalism; yet this is highly surface level, and largely visual, it isn't actually protested. Overall, it's quite straightforward in its messaging, quite literally infantilising a woman, and I don’t have any qualms with it, however, a bit of nuance, or development upon these themes would’ve made the piece a touch more grounding, connecting, perhaps it might’ve helped alleviate the disconnect created by the grotesque body horror. On that, yeah, uhm, the film excels in disgusting me, although, I expected as much and genuinely struggled to convince myself to watch it. More technically, I was pleased in that colour wasn’t shied away from, as is the case frequently in this genre, and in this era; and the camerawork was solid, if albeit a bit uninspired—I also found it notable that some shots were clearly added solely for the sake of evoking disgust, or discomfort, even if the details were irrelevant, most prominently in the opening scenes of the film.

texto: SFF2024 #7 (Closing Night Film) Spends a surprising amount of its third act riffing on extremely specific images from a not very well-regarded Doctor Who episode. This gets a lot of mileage out of its excellent concept, which allows for both lots of squeamishly fun body horror and plenty of (definitely unsubtle but undeniably worthwhile) social commentary about how we view women’s bodies culturally & the speed at which we tend to discard those on our screens once they reach a certain age. To her credit, Fargeat handles the topic deftly without resorting to the self-seriousness that trips up many a horror movie that sets out to say something about a specific issue, though I did feel at times that the film’s camp tone was keeping me at a slight ironic distance from the emotions of the characters. Said characters are brought to life nicely by the cast, though. I don’t think this is quite as much of a Demi Moore showcase as some of the Cannes critics hailed it as (by plot necessity, she’s off-screen for large chunks of the runtime), but it’s certainly bold, electric work from her. There’s a sequence where her character is overcome by body image-related insecurities while getting ready to go out, and it’s made as viscerally heartbreaking as it is by Moore’s excellent work. Margaret Qualley’s material is a bit more one-note but, as usual, she sells it on her screen presence alone (also, at the risk of proving the movie’s point, it must be said that she is quite hot). Dennis Quaid’s turn would be way too much in almost any other movie but it works for this one’s camp sledgehammer of an approach. Fargeat’s cooking with all the right ingredients here, but I think she undercuts herself with self-indulgence. There’s no real reason for this to be 140 minutes long; the concept could have easily made for a brilliant, punchy 90-minutes. By the third act, the movie just keeps piling hats onto hats in service of a gorefest that strays too far from the original allegory. It’s not that it isn’t a natural escalation of the conflict, per se, but I think it’s possible to escalate things a little too much, to the point where it becomes more numbing than impactful. There were several great possible endings in the climax, but Fargeat just kept dragging it out for no apparent reason, and the whole movie - while never boring - is similarly just a bit flabby given the simplicity of its plot. The film’s issues are not big enough to entirely sink it, but they definitely made me feel a bit out of step with the hype from Cannes. As recent Cannes-awarded, women-directed body horrors go, I’m much more of a Titane man.

Unapologetically over the top, unsettling, gut-renching and excessive. At times it felt like never ending stimulation which was often overwhelming. Its strong Sci-fi element is enhanced by interesting designs and is complimented by a very well fitting score and visual aesthetic. All male characters were either hedonistic pigs or lame simps, the latter pretty much always being intolerable, though to its credit added to the unpleasantness of the world. Hyper-sexualisation served its underlying messages and aesthetic, however for me was excessive, although this perspective somewhat changed when I realised how exaggerated the rest movie was also. Denis Quade killed it. While I won’t be watching again, fans of body horror will surely be pleased, as this one takes the genre to new places in the craziest of ways. Well done, Coralie!

texto: 5 stars for the cinematic experience that came with this movie. Without an audience I would have turned this off at the first transitioning scene. Filled with gore, horror, horniness and comedy The Substance was a lot - hence someone in the audience throwing up and fainting in the first 5 minutes of the film which should be taken as a compliment in this shocking genre. A great focus on existentialism and body dysmorphia for women all in hopes to please the embodiment of the rich touchy straight white male - the producer at a sexualised fitness TV program appropriately named Harvey (nice one). Many odes to other films such as The Shining and Trainspotting. Incredibly shot and well acted, I just don’t think this genre is for me. My jaw was on the floor and my ass cheeks were clenched, many sighs of relief when this came to an end.

texto: La serie Z que rezuma. Sobre pinchazos y borbotones. Ya lo escribió Baruch Spinoza en su momento: nadie sabe lo que puede un cuerpo. Transcurrida una hora, me planteo si lo que estoy viendo es una película falsamente subversiva que parte de una idea explícita (la crítica a la sobreexposición del cuerpo femenino en la era del consumo, convertido en producto de carnicería a causa de la tiranía de la belleza) y la lleva al paroxismo. Sin embargo, conforme el relato avanza nos vamos encontrando con una suerte de retorno del espectro de "El hombre elefante", de "Carrie", de "Alien" y de otras múltiples tradiciones del cine norteamericano. Es contundente y celebratoria en el rumbo que toma y también divertida, e incluye una jocosa referencia a "Vertigo".

texto: This film is gonna be a huge divider. All I know is: I won't forget that screening in a hurry. Every Cannes has one: a love it or hate it title that becomes a word-of-mouth sensation thanks to the sheer division it creates among festivalgoers. No, we’re not talking about the so-bad-it-still-isn’t-good Megalopolis, but The Substance, a body horror that goes places even body horror aficionados will be shocked by. Helping this film’s cause are a few things – firstly, it’s the second film from Coralie Fargeat, whose gory thriller Revenge marked her out as one to watch back in 2017 – but, secondly it marks a return-of-sorts for 1990s icon Demi Moore, who is fantastically cast as an ageing Hollywood star who takes a black market drug to create a younger version of herself. The Substance is as gruesome as they come, culminating with an extended sequence that needs to be experienced with a crowd.

texto: Whoa!! This is awesome. Totally insane body horror of the highest order. Filled with the most gratuitously sexual shots of female bodies AND also the most disgustingly gross shots of [redacted] female bodies. It's entertaining as hell! Though the story isn't necessarily anything original (being obsessed with beauty always leads to misery) but the way it's told in THIS film is original. Horror fans are going to lose their shit for this. Rare to see the Cannes press screening audience go THIS wild during a film - that's always the mark of something truly great. If Coralie Fargeat could trim this down by 20 minutes and cut out some of the unnecessarily repetitive shots, this would be an all-timer. It's that close.

texto: Wicked tells the story of Elphaba, a young woman born with green skin—an outcast due to her difference—who arrives at Shiz University. There, she meets Glinda, her polar opposite: popular, privileged, and deeply concerned with her image. Despite their differences, a genuine friendship forms between them as Elphaba gradually discovers that the world of Oz is far less wonderful than it appears. What I found interesting was the way the film questions who gets to decide what is "good" or "bad." Elphaba is rejected before she has even done anything, simply because she is different. Conversely, Glinda fits the mold of the "perfect" girl: beautiful, popular, and well-liked. Yet, as the story unfolds, this contrast becomes far less clear-cut. The relationship between the two is clearly one of the film’s highlights. They represent two completely different ways of responding to how others perceive them: Elphaba ultimately accepts rejection rather than compromising her convictions, whereas Glinda is far more invested in validation and popularity. Visually, I really enjoyed the world-building. Oz is incredibly colorful, intricately designed, and almost fairytale-like, featuring a striking contrast between Glinda’s bright, pink aesthetic and the darker tones associated with Elphaba. The costumes and sets give the film a strong identity, and the musical numbers are clearly designed as full-scale spectacles. However, despite all this, I felt the film sometimes lacked the depth it seemed to promise. While certain themes—such as discrimination and propaganda—are interesting, they remain somewhat simplistic. The film spends a great deal of time establishing its world and characters, which can make the story feel like it is moving rather slowly at times. The fact that this is only the first part of the story also reinforces this impression. We reach the end just as several plotlines are barely getting started. This is understandable, given that the film is designed as the first chapter, but as a standalone movie, I find it makes the experience less satisfying. Spoiler (ending): Elphaba finally discovers that the Wizard and Madame Morrible are manipulating events in Oz—specifically using the plight of the Animals to consolidate their power. She refuses to be part of this system and flees, while Glinda remains in Oz. Elphaba is then publicly branded a threat. However, the "Defying Gravity" scene is brilliantly executed; it perfectly captures Elphaba’s choice: she would rather be seen as wicked than conform to others' expectations of her. Ultimately, I found *Wicked* interesting and visually stunning, with excellent chemistry between the two female leads, yet I was left wanting a bit more regarding the story and the depth of certain themes. There was immense potential, but I was more impressed by the world-building and the spectacle than truly moved by the narrative itself.

texto: Best moment: “Defying gravity”. That song and scene is the centerpiece of the musical and this (and the other) movie. It doesn’t disappoint. The song by itself already feels epic but the movie version puts a cherry on top. This small action interlude on the broom is a fun little break before it works toward that climax and note we have all been waiting for. Best quote: “I don’t cause commotions. I am one.” MVP: Cynthia Erivo. First, her voice is stunning. It is so crystal clear and she switches between emotional to powerful with the flip of vocal cord. Second, the acting matches the vocal performance. She gives Elphaba so much heart and a deep compassion but that fury beneath the surface is always brewing. It is an emotional performance in all areas. Best visual: The wizard’s room. The rest of the movie is so bright, colorful and joyful. That set, however, is darker and there isn’t any of the joy of the Emerald City. The design of the big head also looks really cool and ominous. Best showstopper: “Dancing through life” is just so much fun. The part in the library has so much cool choreography with the books and the spinning set. The ballroom looks stunning and also has some fun choreography. In all of this I ask myself one important question: How can someone be as charming as Jonathan Bailey? Rating: 9 out of 10 flying monkeys

texto: This is hardly a femme fatale story. More like a tale of extreme marital dysfunction and some lost soul that gets twisted up in it. The phrase ‘country girl’ seems to be used as a euphemism for prostitute or someone lesser. Myeong-ja spends the whole time trying to find increasingly extreme ways of responding to trauma, leading to disaster not entirely of her own making. I also didn’t quite get the commentary in the beginning regarding the aggressive youth in the post-Cold War environment, referring to the crazed teenagers unrelated to the household crime. The scene didn’t quite translate to the main character story at all but seemed to be given a particular weight regardless.

texto: M(a)y Korea Challenge 2025 38. SK Drama A completely superfluous remake of The Housemaid which is worse in every way. The maid gets a new backstory and Youn Yuh-jung, in her debut role, plays her as if "girl from the country" was a mental disorder. Less of a threatening sexual force she is just another broken trauma doll, infantile and ready to be abused. Overall, the menacing presence of female agency is replaced by brute masculine force (read: rape scenes, endowed with a giallo -esque visual flair). The "cautionary tale" framing narrative of the previous version, with its charmingly bizarre final scene, is traded for a clichéed police investigation. And since the children play no role at all, and simply disappear after a few early scenes, I even miss Ahn Sung-Ki's bratty antics. Nah; this was an unnecessary disappointment.

texto: Myeong-ja convinced me to drink rat poison. I haven't seen The Housemaid by the same director and I think that's a bit of a problem as this is a heavily stylised and hysterically acted variation on the film he laid down over a decade earlier. Everything here has a melodrama turned up to the highest settings and the cast's performances become so flailing and ridiculous that you wonder if the film is insisting on not being taken seriously. What's more most of the cool stylisation is really front loaded and that's before the dialogue completely goes to crazy town so you're left with a first half that routinely looks really interesting and a tone which is off-kilter but not completely lost and then a second half where people are just having wild emotional swings and routinely falling in to complete hysteria in sets you've now seen a dozen times with lighting that can only be described as generic. The final sequence with two of the characters still manipulating future events whilst dying from having ingested rat poison did win me back a bit though. I'm still sat here having no clue what the film was even trying to do which makes critiquing it quite hard. Freya's rating: 1/5

texto: 《下女》裡傭人主動引誘金先生，敢於表達慾望、抽煙當壞女孩；《火女》裡則是主人借醉強暴傭人，鄉下女子來城市，願望是找個好老公，補完《下女》缺乏描述之處。仲介所樓梯是通往不同階層的道路。家庭是串連起整部電影的關鍵，女子要守清白之身，為日後要嫁人；出軌的丈夫一身臭味，婚外情性關係意味髒亂。暴露當日韓國社會保守。丈夫向妻子告白自己的出軌事跡，遭妻子唾棄，反指責妻子為何不能像其他人的妻子一樣放下瑣事，助丈夫發展事業。忍忍讓讓，都是為了維持中產家庭的運作。血案發生，纏糾結束。最後留下來面對悲劇的，還是已飽遭傷害的女性。尹汝貞處女作，不懂她在裡面演出是出於本意還是經過金綺泳調教，總整體而言，《火女》多有讓人浮誇失真。碎屍瘋癲，比《下女》多了幾分邪典的味道。

texto: Second time around, it’s easy to spot all the ways Bong Joon-ho cribbed from peak Kim Ki-young: the family house here, in particular, appears a direct inspiration for Parasite , the production design evoking the same note of extravagance that never quite crosses over into the unreal. There are parallels with Minari too, though, in the slightly peculiar amount of time spent on the raising of chickens, and the ‘smell’ of Youn Yuh-jung’s character (Namkoong Won holds his nose the first time he encounters her). This was her debut performance, and it has to be said that it shows: she has this habit of jutting out her teeth in every reaction shot, and it’s distracting as hell. Youn has said that she didn’t enjoy working with Kim, and on the evidence it’s easy to see why: he treats the actors less like people than as vessels for the projection of his ideas. With this semi-remake of The Housemaid , it’s almost as if he set out to recreate that film in crash course form. His obsessions coalesce into florid extremities, whereas the brutally compressed plot beats make little sense without the context of the earlier counterpart. For something so drenched in arch style, I think the most impactful and memorable moment is, ironically, the final scene: an unvarnished outpouring of emotion, heightened by the stark use of white. Seen at the Korean Film Archive's Youn Yuh-jung retrospective, 7 May 2021

texto: Asian Cinema Challenge 2024: boxd.it/rgmNA 4. Korean Film Archive Top 100 Future Academy Award winner Youn Yuh-jung made her debut in Kim Ki-young's psychedelic remix/reworking/reshuffle (take your pick) of his superior 1960 film The Housemaid. With its Argento-esque colours and manic imagery, Woman of Fire has some subtle differences in approach to the monochrome melodrama The Housemaid. But I don't think this remake of sorts adds much to the original. Both are about sin, although the 1971 film cranks up the sultriness whereas the original pressed forth the dissolution of the family dynamic. But The Housemaid feels fresher and it cranks up the tension more gradually than the psychosexual Woman of Fire.

texto: I do love a good love triangle in Korean cinema, it always promises to be a good, but bonkers, time. This movie doesn’t take long to start going off the rails and it stays off the rails in some impressive ways throughout the rest of the movie. The acing is over the top but it matches the aggressive use of color and camera work that dominate the aesthetic style of this movie. I do think that the movie is probably a little bit too fast paced (there isn’t enough exposition at times), but it’s hard to keep your eyes off of what is happening on screens and all of the elements are working well together.

texto: «Женщина в огне» – первый авторемейк эпохальной «Горничной» Ким Ги-ёна (второй выйдет спустя одиннадцать лет), своеобразная ревизия общественных нравов, выполняемая режиссером раз в десятилетие. Для корейских кинематографистов «Hanyo» стала настольной библией, а ее сюжет стал бродячим, плотно войдя в кинематографический канон. Новая версия культовой картины, вошедшая в мизогиническую трилогию, очевидно, снята под большим влиянием джалло, в отличие от строгого по форме черно-белого оригинала первый авторемейк изобилует всеми оттенками взрывных красного и синего, а квартирные интерьеры становятся объектом эстетизации. Ким Ги-ён или как его прозвали на родине «господин Монстр» выходит на пик своей творческой формы, снимая предельно экзальтированные картины, смешивающие особенности корейского менталитета, насилие, разрушение семьи, сексуальные девиации, женобоязнь и дикие сюрреалистические образы. В «Hwanyeo» режиссер немного отходит в сторону от социальных аллегорий оригинала, делая акцент на психологической подоплеке поступков героев – они идут вразнос, чтобы постепенно сойти с ума. С наступлением Четвертой республики в стране уже установилась цензура, поэтому кореец выбирает самое надежное укрытие – в глубине жанровых картин, но его персонажи по-прежнему зловещи и пугающи, балансируя на грани откровенной карикатуры и звериной монструозности. Дебютантка Юн Ё-Дзён, сыгравшая коварную деревенскую простушку, открыла галерею чудовищ в женском обличье в самом ярком творческом десятилетии режиссера, но в отличие от злодейки из первого фильма, поступки героини, выбравшей проторить себе путь наверх по социальной лестнице, обоснованы ненавистью в сторону мира мужчин, уже жестоко обошедшегося с девушкой. Ким Ги-ён вставляет в самые кульминационные моменты звук удара по раскаленному железу (постоянно напоминающий героине о чудовищном моменте из прошлого), вместе с кислотной цветовой палитрой и чередой взрывных экспрессионистских образов они окаймляют психологические перверсии, разрушающие шаткий мир корейской семьи, свято чтящей патриархат и встроенной в жесткое капиталистическое общество. Колесо смерти набирает обороты, руки героев окрашиваются кровью, безумие уже замерло на пороге. Новая версия классовой «Служанки» мутирует в психоделическую мелодраму о женщинах и мужчинах на грани нервного срыва, незваная гостья, обуреваемая стыдом и желанием, преследуемая психологической травмой, срывает маски с благопристойных членов корейского общества, как огня боящихся разоблачения и потери статуса. Если в оригинале Ким Ги-ён выводил на экране кровожадных паучих, рвущих мужчину на части, чтобы сделать его марионеткой в своих руках, то в «Женщина в огне» превращает героиню в разносящую по дому заразу крысу, искажая внутренний мир хозяев дома, забывающих о всех моральных ценностях и превращающихся в зверей. В картине есть как грех, так и искупление, как похоть, так и невинность, как отчаяние, так и смирение. Но благообразная маска успешной семьи, чей социальный капитал гораздо важнее любви и преданности, уже треснула, поэтому вой оставшейся в живых перебивает звон ненавистного металла. Грязное, извращенное и одновременно притягивающее к себе зрелище.

texto: Woman of Fire | Kim Ki-young | 1971 | 2024 Asian Cinema Season - Film 130 "You may have taken my life but my soul... I cannot give it to you." Kim Ki-young’s Woman of Fire (1971) reimagines his earlier film The Housemaid (1960) with a continued focus on class, gender, and the darker aspects of human nature. The film tells the story of Myeong-Ja, a young woman from the countryside who becomes a maid for the Dong-Sik family in Seoul. Her presence disrupts the family’s stability, revealing the underlying tensions and hypocrisies of their lives. Myeong-Ja is not just a disruptor but a symbol of the hidden forces within society that challenge the status quo. Her actions expose the vulnerabilities and pretences of the Dong-Sik family, highlighting the personal conflicts and moral decay in their household. The transition from rural to urban life, depicted through Myeong-Ja’s journey, reflects her struggle and the shifting dynamics within the family. "When you autopsy human nature, black blood will flow out. That is what we call desire." – Kim Ki-young The film critiques the patriarchal and hierarchical structures of the family. The male characters, though outwardly powerful, are often weak and morally corrupt. Dong-Sik, the husband, succumbs to a destructive affair with Myeong-Ja, symbolising his moral decay and the fragility of his authority. His affair with Myeong-Ja is a catalyst that brings to light the suppressed desires and frustrations within the household. What drives a person to abandon their moral compass for fleeting desires? The use of colour, especially reds and blues, symbolises the intense emotions and tensions within the household. Red, in particular, points to passion, violence, and the blood ties that bind and destroy the characters. This vivid use of colour heightens the film’s dramatic impact, making it a visual spectacle that draws the audience into its emotional core. One of the film's most compelling aspects is its portrayal of women. Myeong-Ja, initially a victim of her circumstances, evolves into a powerful figure who challenges the established order. Her actions force the other characters, and the audience, to confront uncomfortable truths about gender roles and societal expectations. How far will someone go to assert their agency in a world that seeks to suppress them? The film was released during a time of significant political and social change in South Korea. Censorship was rife, and filmmakers had to navigate these restrictions carefully. Kim Ki-young cleverly uses visual metaphors and indirect storytelling to bypass censorship, allowing him to explore provocative themes without explicit content. Scenes of sexual tension and violence are often depicted through shadows, reflections, and suggestive imagery, enhancing the film’s psychological impact while complying with censorship laws. Woman of Fire also explores themes of power and control within the intimate setting of the household. The Dong-Sik family’s attempt to maintain their social status and control over their environment ultimately leads to their downfall. This internal struggle reflects the broader societal tensions of maintaining appearances versus confronting hidden truths. While Woman of Fire is a powerful and significant work in its own right, it is perhaps somewhat derivative of Kim's earlier film, The Housemaid. The core narrative and thematic elements are revisited and expanded upon, which might make the film feel familiar to those who have seen the original. However, this does not diminish the film’s impact; instead, it offers a deeper, more stylised exploration of similar themes. The film can be seen as an evolution of Kim's ideas, where he refines his critique of societal norms and human desires. In my view, Woman of Fire stands out for its thematic depth and historical relevance. Kim Ki-young dissects societal structures with a keen eye, presenting a narrative that explores the complexities of human nature. The film's ability to provoke thought and challenge perceptions makes it a powerful piece of cinema that continues to resonate with audiences today. Its influence is evident in contemporary Korean cinema, inspiring films like Parasite that similarly critique social hierarchies and human desires.

texto: Asian Cinema Challenge 2024: boxd.it/rgmNA 4. Korean Film Archive Top 100 Future Academy Award winner Youn Yuh-jung made her debut in Kim Ki-young's psychedelic remix/reworking/reshuffle (take your pick) of his superior 1960 film The Housemaid. With its Argento-esque colours and manic imagery, Woman of Fire has some subtle differences in approach to the monochrome melodrama The Housemaid. But I don't think this remake of sorts adds much to the original. Both are about sin, although the 1971 film cranks up the sultriness whereas the original pressed forth the dissolution of the family dynamic. But The Housemaid feels fresher and it cranks up the tension more gradually than the psychosexual Woman of Fire.

texto: This film didn’t do much for me. It leaned heavily into excessive melodrama and soap-opera energy, but without much bite to justify all the heightened emotions. I went in expecting something closer to Suddenly In The Dark (1981), with that kind of bonkers, spiraling intensity. Unfortunately, Woman of Fire never really got to that level of wildness. There were moments where the crime and thriller elements briefly flared up, and those scenes showcased the sharper and more electrifying film this could have been. But most of the runtime sinked into melodrama instead, which left me more detached than engrossed.

texto: I have to respect a director who does a remake of a film he himself made only about a decade prior, but takes it in such a stylistically different direction. Personally, I preferred The Housemaid, but that doesn't take anything away from what was accomplished here; there seemed to be far less empathizing with the patriarch and far more agency lended to his wife, as well as a considerable amount of vibrant, sorta psychedelic use of color. It's nothing totally new, yet nothing too redundant.

texto: Performances are so hammy and overdone (which I fully believe is intentional) that I think it undermines the visual flourishes. IMO, inserting still-image montage, subjective techniques, jarring color choices into an otherwise more subdued narrative style is more interesting. What Kim Ki-young does here makes the melodramatic scenes feel flattened. Idk if there's truly anything new here, and tbh I think I prefer the abject misery and disjoint of INSECT WOMAN. Still very fascinating that Kim Ki-young made a masterpiece in 1960 and spent his career trying to remake the same story (often with the same actors).

texto: A quintessentially seventies film as The Housemaid was a quintessentially sixties film. It’s The Housemaid on acid. It falls into a lot of the narrative traps that its predecessor so tactfully avoided, but it almost seems intentional; Kim destroys the spaces between plot points in such a way that feels nightmarish and irrational. Hope to pick up a lot of the buried symbolism on second watch.

texto: Second time around, it’s easy to spot all the ways Bong Joon-ho cribbed from peak Kim Ki-young: the family house here, in particular, appears a direct inspiration for Parasite , the production design evoking the same note of extravagance that never quite crosses over into the unreal. There are parallels with Minari too, though, in the slightly peculiar amount of time spent on the raising of chickens, and the ‘smell’ of Youn Yuh-jung’s character (Namkoong Won holds his nose the first time he encounters her). This was her debut performance, and it has to be said that it shows: she has this habit of jutting out her teeth in every reaction shot, and it’s distracting as hell. Youn has said that she didn’t enjoy working with Kim, and on the evidence it’s easy to see why: he treats the actors less like people than as vessels for the projection of his ideas. With this semi-remake of The Housemaid , it’s almost as if he set out to recreate that film in crash course form. His obsessions coalesce into florid extremities, whereas the brutally compressed plot beats make little sense without the context of the earlier counterpart. For something so drenched in arch style, I think the most impactful and memorable moment is, ironically, the final scene: an unvarnished outpouring of emotion, heightened by the stark use of white. Seen at the Korean Film Archive's Youn Yuh-jung retrospective, 7 May 2021

texto: Going into this, I hadn't realized this is was supposed to be a remake in essence of Kim Ki-young's own seminal film The Housemaid from a decade prior. I also didn't know this was Youn Yuh-jung's first film, and she is an absolute scene stealer in this. The ending became a little overly dramatic and unnecessary complicated for my taste, but still a worthwhile watch.

texto: A distinct enough remake of the original The Housemaid with amped up moral decline and some very interesting camerawork. The psychedelic imagery didn’t really do it for me personally, but was a unique touch. The altered story felt less real but allows Myeong-Ja to develop into an arguably more compelling femme fatale. Overall, I prefer the original, but this one is still enjoyable.

texto: A remake/retelling of Kim's own film, The Housemaid (1960). Whereas the earlier movie addresses the concerns of creeping materialism into Korean society in the aftermath of the war, Woman of Fire uses the same narrative to plot a more sexually-charged tale focusing on the exploitation and subjugation of women in a highly conservative and patriarchal society. Woman of Fire is a gripping and evocative story which focuses on bodily autonomy, inter-relation power dynamics and violence towards women which, sadly, still feels rather topical even whilst watching this in 2020. Mixing elements of horror and melodrama, this is a highly engaging movie which (alongside Kim's other films) have had a clear and deep impact on modern Korean cinema - watching this, we can see the direct influence it had on Bong Joon-ho's Parasite. It is a deep shame that Kim Ki-yong's films have yet to find themselves included in the established canon of popular world cinema but, with Parasite providing a belated breakthrough for Korean cinema onto the world stage, belated recognition for one of the most unique voices in movie history is a distinct possibility.

texto: Second installment of Kim Ki-Young’s Housemaid trilogy and this one is louder, macabre, and more unforgiving than its predecessor. Youn Yuh-Jung is so entertaining in her debut it’s no wonder that she is recognized with an Oscar. Since the 60s was a Golden Age of Cinema then the 70s was Darkness — Korea’s government dominated and repressed what could be released into media. I’m surprised and grateful to watch some crazy shit that happens in this movie. What happens when you restrain creativity? It needs a release.

texto: Kim Ki-young actualitza el seu clàssic de 1960 amb un color sobresaturat més uns personatges i trama encara més retorçats. Beu de Hitchcock però és més moderna tant en posada en escena com en muntatge. Curiós veure com ja hi són presents la cruesa i les hipèrboles narratives que podem veure en autors coreans d'aquest segle com Kim Jee-woon, Park Chan-wook, o Kim Ki-duk. A més, és el primer paper de la llegendària actriu Youn Yuh-jung, pel qual va guanyar el premi Blue Dragon a millor actriu.

texto: First movie where I can say there’s a Checkov’s meat grinder. Radical departure from Kim Ki Young’s original version of the Housemaid, this version leans more towards exploitation, grindhouse and even a bit of Giallo while still keeping true to the melodrama of his first take on the story. Vivid color and lighting with some gorgeous stills montages of the killings in order to get around the censorship of the 70s dictatorship. Wild ride all the way through.
